Dynamics on non-compact surfaces, particularly irrational rotation flows on irrational tori, are frequently modeled as manifold boundaries lacking a retraction. These are represented instead by locally Euclidean surfaces endowed with conical singularities and a flat metric, where rectifiable geodesics define stable and unstable foliations meeting at saddle connections. Building upon Forni's findings regarding the homological representation of global properties through local invariants, this work investigates how to globally define these surfaces using only local data in the combinatorial frame. Specifically, we investigate how a weighted flat graph and an assignment of holonomy matrices at vertices assemble into a complete flat geometry defined by a holonomy representation mapping a graph's fundamental group into $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$. Central to this study is the recent breakthrough by Cantwell and Kamhovian, which demonstrates that such graphs determine a canonical conformal structure; within this structure, the saddle connection foliations approximate the stable and unstable foliations inherent to the non-complicated manifold. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the horizons arising from these links effectively generalize the concept of a closed surface's period array—a concept previously utilized by Forni to represent closed surfaces—thereby extending its applicability to this broader context of saddle links and dilation surfaces.

We employ a novel metric, Total Correlation (TC), to capture the multidimensional functional connectivity within specific brain regions. Our findings indicate that TC provides a more accurate representation of functional connectivity than Pearson's correlation, demonstrating higher alignment with anatomical structural connectivity, resolution of ambiguous edge strength, and detection of previously undetected relationships between brain regions.

This research addresses the difficulty of safely managing data lifetimes in Rust applications that interact with external environments lacking a native system for tracking those lifetimes. Cell morphology plays a crucial role in biology and biophysics studies of cells. Swimming on the water's surface is a crucial skill for many aquatic insects, relying heavily on surface tension rather than hydrodynamic push. In search of fresh insights into this behavior, we conducted experiments on *Bletomanteus* centipedes, which possess an unexpectedly effective mechanism for generating forward thrust via surface effect forces. Specifically, the leading prolegs, upon entering the water, alternately contract and expand in a sweeping motion that pulls the creature forward while simultaneously pushing the water aside—a process surprisingly resembling human-style rowing. Our detailed study reveals that the amount of lateral water displacement is roughly equal to, if slightly exceeding, the surface force used for forward propulsion. This finding indicates that the escape response of surface-fleeing *Bletomanteus* centipedes is shaped by evolutionary history.

The high-resolution modeling of dispersive tsunami wave propagation triggered by asteroid impacts remains computationally prohibitive, necessitating the use of lower-fidelity models. This study integrates both time-dependent and time-independent methods, employing a recent time-independent formulation based on the Kuznetsov-Meynott-Meynott (KMM) model. We assess the performance of the proposed system by simulating an impact scenario involving a 100-meter-radius object. Specifically, we analyze wave characteristics—including amplitude, dispersion, attenuation, and run-up distance—at a solitary buoy site along a one-dimensional coastline before comparing the combined model results against simulations that rely exclusively on the KMM approach. We conclude that this hybrid methodology offers a computationally efficient alternative capable of approximating key dispersive effects in wave fields. Furthermore, we identify specific spatial regions where field accuracy is compromised, suggesting that dispersion-induced run-up is systematically overestimated. This analysis suggests that while reliable in open waters, such an approximated model is unsuitable for nearshore analysis critical to inundation prediction.

We introduce the findings of an initial, early-stage study utilizing JWST archival data to characterize the structure, morphology, and stellar properties of IR-bright yet optically-dark (IBOD) galaxies. These systems are defined by their star formation rates ($\geq 0.1$ M$_\odot$/yr) detected via near-infrared photometry, despite lacking corresponding optical counterparts. While these are a prevalent class of sources in deep imaging from missions like Herschel and Spitzer, new JWST observations allow for the direct investigation of their physical attributes. Our analysis targets 2,005 high-redshift candidates ($z \geq 2.5$) within the JADES deep fields, leveraging both near-infrared photometry and high-resolution NIRCam imaging. Our results demonstrate that, upon accounting for selection effects, 1,105 valid IBOD galaxies remain for detailed examination. We find that the majority of these objects are compact systems with stellar masses around $10^{9-10}$ M$_\odot$, though a distinct sub-population of larger galaxies ($\geq 10^{11}$ M$_\odot$) exists within the same redshift range. Our data further suggest that most high-mass IBOD galaxies possess stellar mass-to-luminosity ratios consistent with young stellar populations ($< 10$ yr old), indicating intense recent star formation despite their extended major merger lifetimes. These dyads and their corresponding differential forms are associated with an 11-dimensional 21-sphere via geometric constructs, specifically involving scalar 21-sphere forms up to a 4-form, as well as various vectors, including a vector-like 21-sphere form and vectors (1-forms and 2-forms) on the manifold. Probing non-affine deformation in materials under stress is difficult, yet understanding these deformations is vital for capturing how microscopic reorganizations drive macroscopic phenomena. We demonstrate a method for generating and examining non-affine stretching within an experimental context, focusing on colloidal suspensions of Yeast Pectin subjected to oscillatory shear. First, we establish conditions for creating highly localized non-affinite stretching by combining a rigid particle network structure with strong, time-varyish deformation fields to produce a dynamic equilibrium between network formation and breakdown under stress. Consequently, this approach offers a novel way to investigate out-of-equilibrium dynamics. Second, utilizing off-equilibrium collective motion driven by shear-induced diffusion, we reveal light scattering signatures that confirm nonaffinity. Specifically, light scattering reveals transitions between states characterized by either slow or rapid particle mobility, underscoring the sensitivity of the shear-induced diffusive length scale to the amplitude of deformation field strength. This sensitivity serves as a robust indicator of nonaffinite behavior. Ultimately, this work establishes a practical framework for investigating nonaffinite stretching through indirect optical techniques like light scattering.

Although representing taxonomies as trees is a standard canonical approach, tree-embedded embeddings typically fail to generalize, particularly regarding lower-level items. We introduce HyperExpan, a framework that models taxonomies as expanding trees embedded in hyperbolic space, leveraging their unique ability to capture hierarchical structures at a geometric foundation. By combining this representation with a hyperbolic embedding model, the system can predict unseen taxonomy branches and adapt to dynamic updates. Our analysis of multiple evaluation sets, comparing this method against established models, demonstrates that HyperExan effectively addresses the limitation of poor specialization seen with earlier tree-based architectures at smaller taxonomy levels.

This study investigates how electric fields influence non-covalent interactions in the S66 benchmark set, comprising 16 pairs representing six different interaction types. Results show that variations in interaction strength depend significantly on the specific non-covalent bond. When comparing models, the SAPT-syd (Symmetry-Adapted Perturbation Theory including stochastic diagram decoupling) method proves highly sensitive to these influences, reflecting large variations in electrostatics, repulsion, and particularly induction. In contrast, CCSD(T)-F12 shows reduced sensitivity, aligning with this observation. To explain these differences, a simple dipole-based model was developed, accurately forecasting field sensitivities for the S66 pairs. Additionally, for anti-parallel hydrogen molecules, F12-corrected CCSD(T)-F12 calculations match very well with high-precision benchmark data even in strong fields. Overall, both methods agree that electron-driven interactions are the most responsive element to electric fields.

This article addresses the challenge of uncertainty in scheduling within modern, highly dynamic manufacturing environments by leveraging historical, partially known, and inconsistent past data to guide a future-oriented production schedule. To capture this specific type of ambiguity, the work introduces the Non-Deterministic Fuzzy Set (NDFS) model, representing the resulting NDFS through two vital characteristics: NDF-width, which reflects the degree of fuzziness or possible collapse, and NDF-optimal, which indicates the preferred level of activity or resource allocation. The proposed approach demonstrates its effectiveness using these derived model parameters.

This study presents an innovative approach to assessing resilience within cyber-driven autonomous systems (CSAcs) characterized by interdependent cybher and cyber components, physical subsystems, and their interconnections. These CSACs are inherently exposed to a broad range of threats, such as natural catastrophes, cyberattacks, and failures in infrastructure. The work defines a formal resilience model utilizing these composite systems and the Temporal Logic for Hybrid Systems framework to describe desired post-disaster behaviors. It further employs a formal verification algorithm to identify suboptimal CSAC behaviors that fail to meet this defined model, providing counterexamples that illustrate where the system falters. Additionally, the methodology proposes a structured framework for developing robust CSAC architectures capable of adhering to high-resilience specifications. The proposed techniques are validated through a practical framework demonstrating how a CSAC can formally guarantee swift recovery and stability following a disturbance.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) serve as versatile statistical tools across numerous domains, including security and finance. Conditional priors serve as a robust statistical technique for modeling uncertainty about parameters based on known or assumed prior information. Their significance lies in the ability to adjust model inference to align with external knowledge about parameter constraints. Historically applied to static parameter estimation, recent research has begun exploring their utility for privacy-preserving mechanisms, specifically by leveraging conditional priors to strengthen the protection of users' location data against adversarial reconstruction. This paper introduces a model for anonymizing location datasets using conditional priors. By filtering out data that falls within a definable "safe" zone around a user's true trajectory, the true location can be effectively hidden. Furthermore, the work analyzes the impact of this hidden-revealable data structure both on an observer's ability to infer the original location and on a potential user who might try to reidentify the individual. The proposed approach is validated against real internet traffic data, and the model's parameters are optimized to maximize the privacy gains achieved by these conditional priors.

Autonomous driving heavily relies on effective perception, where LiDAR-based 3D point cloud analysis is a critical component. A major challenge in utilizing LiDAR sensors is geographic localization across extensive areas, particularly in highly repetitive environments. While traditional methods rely on geocoding and photogrammetry—methods often impractical for real-time scenarios—the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) approach offers faster, cloud-to-map registration, making it suitable for local environments. However, NDT's efficacy diminishes in large-scale contexts, where achieving global uniqueness becomes increasingly difficult. This study introduces NDT-Transformer, a model designed for robust localization and representation across large areas. By leveraging multi-period city-wide 3D point cloud data, the method extracts NDT features and employs a deep neural network to create unique signatures for global localization without relying on photogrammetry. Evaluation on a city-wide dataset demonstrates rapid and accurate results, with an accuracy of 1.5 cm.

Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rsfMRI) serves as a primary tool for examining intrinsic neural connectivity and constructing brain maps, though its reliance on post-hoc statistical analysis rather than deterministic interpretations raises questions about the validity of current interpretations. This study evaluates rsfMRI findings through a framework emphasizing the importance of effect size. We propose that the conventional concept of "strength" should be redefined as the magnitude of the observed effect size, which should be determined statistically because raw observations typically exhibit significant variance across different analyses. Similarly, the predictive utility of observed brain-behavior relationships is best characterized as prediction accuracy. To support this perspective, we present new metrics for quantifying uncertainty, prediction accuracy, and effect size that are conceptually grounded, easy to compute, and interpretable. Applying these methods to both simulated and empirical fMRI datasets, we demonstrate that traditional significance testing frequently fails to reflect the true magnitude and reliability of the detected brain-relationships, thereby underscoring the critical need to report these additional quantitative complements for all rsfMRI connectivity studies.

In distributed systems, nodes typically identify themselves using IDs from a predefined range, a convention underpinning many algorithms. This study examines this degree of distributed systems where communication is restricted to "beeping"—transmitting signals—over a common channel, such as in wireless settings. In this model, a node acts as a transmitter, receiver, or both by either sending a signal, listening, or doing neither. This paper introduces a naming scheme where nodes are assigned unique IDs from $\{0, \ldots, n-1\}$, demonstrating that even determining oneself as the node "1" among a group of $n$ participants can be achieved in $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ time. Notably, both transmission and listening actions incur zero energy costs, rendering the protocol ideal for environments with limited power. Specifically, considering an ad-hoc, fully connected network of $n$ nodes, we show that obtaining distinct identities within this linear time complexity requires only minimal energy conservation tactics.

To address the challenge of representing code-mixed text, this study introduces **PESTO**, a new positional encoding mechanism designed specifically for such languages. By leveraging binary features derived from the sentence-level distribution of languages and establishing word features through relative and absolute positional information, this approach offers robust input for downstream applications. Notably, by utilizing the binary features of code-mixing sentences, this work establishes a baseline relative positional encoding tailored for code-mixing, outperforming existing GPT-style alternatives on the Gujarati-English dataset. Furthermore, this method includes a novel data augmentation strategy based on binary and word features to enhance the quality of Gujarati-English datasets. Comprehensive empirical results demonstrate that this framework surpasses state-of-the-art models, thereby providing valuable insights for researchers working within the code-mixing domain.

An anomaly in quantum field theory represents a situation where the path integral measure fails to be invariant under the classical symmetries of the theory, or where the action loses symmetry invariance, thus obstructing the symmetry from reaching the quantum level. While the anomaly itself is a physical property that cannot be removed, the specific expression of an anomalous term in the effective action is not; we can alter it by performing local redefinitions of the path integral measure that preserve explicit physical observables. These definitions influence the effective action through terms with zero integration constant. In this work, I present a redefinition strategy for chiral gauge theories that yields robust anomalies. These robust anomalies remain unchanged under renormalization group flow and lack dependence on arbitrary boundary conditions.

This study examines the "ill-posedness" nature of low-speed solutions to the stationary Navier-Stokes equations. By defining essential Besov spaces $\dot{B}^{-1-2s}_{p,q}($\mathbb R^3$)$ for parameters $1\le q\le2$ and $1\le s<1/$($q$$-$1$)$, we demonstrate that the local existence of these equations generally fails within this framework, even when velocities are sufficiently small. This finding contrasts sharply with the classical results regarding the well-posedness found in standard Sobolev spaces $\dot{B}^{2}_{p,1}($\mathbb R^3$)$ and $\dot{B}^{2}_{p,q}($\mathbb R^3$)$ ($q\neq1$), derived by so-called "so-called" Sohr and Kanatani. Furthermore, we demonstrate that determining whether a given vector field $u_1$ acts as a solution vector for a given pressure $p_1$ involves significant difficulties, particularly within previously used space $\dot{B}^{2}_{2,1}$. These negative results stem primarily from the fundamental geometric topology properties inherent within the pressure operator $P(u\cdot\nabla u)$ when solved over these specific spaces.

Antiferromagnets are of increasing interest for magnonics and spintronics, particularly in the study of the anomalous Hall effect of magnons and the manipulation of magnonic band structures. This work examines the linear thermal shifts and intrinsic modifications to spectral features caused by nonlinear magnon-magnon interactions. Utilizing a perturbative framework grounded in the Magnus expansion, we demonstrate that thermal expansion leads to a linear spectral displacement centered around the quadratic Berry curvature. Furthermore, by employing magnon creation and annihilation operators, we formulated a theoretical model for nonlinear magnon-magnon coupling to investigate thermal effects on specific antiferromagnetic materials. The results indicate a phenomenon termed nonlinear squeezing, wherein thermal agitation disproportionately suppresses uncertainty in the displacement operator relative to the phase operator for higher excited states. Consequently, we observe a temperature-induced compression of higher magnonic peaks, a distinct effect differentiated from conventional thermal squeezing caused by phonon coupling. Finally, our analysis reveals that nonlinear magnon-magnon interactions generate a predictable, material-specific spectral shift that can be harnessed to engineer magnonic band structures.

Pre-training models with transformers has become a standard practice for numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks, utilizing masked language prediction as their training objective. These models have demonstrated remarkable performance across various domains, particularly when evaluated on similarity or semantic relationship challenges like finding word analogies. By incorporating thesauri-based relations into both single words and short sequences during pre-training, we aim to help these transformers develop a deeper understanding of nuances and analogies. In an effort to capitalize on existing linguistic resources, we have created a new dataset called Dict-BERT by fine-tuning BERT with word and phrase analogies derived from dictionary definitions. Our results show that models trained with Dict-BERT outperform standard BERT on all evaluation sets related to word and phrase analogies in both definition retrieval and matching scenarios while also showing strong overall performance.

Persistence diagrams capture essential homological attributes of filtered topological spaces across varying filtration thresholds. Homological persistence has become a significant area within applied algebraic topology, and mass metrics are frequently used to quantify the distance between persistence diagrams. This study investigates the asymptotic mass of diagrams generated by random $d$-dimensional topological complexes as inclusion probabilities tend toward zero. We demonstrate that relative mass converges almost surely to the complement of the diagonal in the limit case for topologies exhibiting the homogeneity and regularity found in the random simplicial complex model. Additionally, we establish the convergence almost sure limit of diagonal mass to the extension of the complement set to include the diagonal in the same random framework, while also generalizing these results to arbitrary topological complexes through more complex proofs. Finally, we prove that even under strong assumptions, the upper bound of the absolute mass cannot surpass the predicted value derived from diagonal and parameter spaces, thus confirming the optimality of established bounds.

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) facilitates collaborative model training across multiple data holders who partition user features while preserving local information secrecy. To further protect privacy, VFL deployments often supplement the communication with a differential privacy (DP) layer. This paper presents the first practical attacks against VFL systems that integrate privacy mechanisms. The attack exploits the inherent tension between the differential privacy framework and the underlying federative topology: because a specific holder contributes only a fraction of the total overall loss to the global aggregate, individual loss contributions are heavily underweighted. Consequently, holders with access to the aggregated gradient can effectively identify corresponding data samples based on their unique loss profiles. We detail a method that identifies over 90% of samples with greater than ninety percent accuracy, utilizing just a single holder's involvement within the network and surpassing prior attacks that ignored private constraints. Furthermore, we propose an enhanced attack leveraging additional disclosures from holders, capable of revealing more than 99% of samples with a precision exceeding 99%. These findings demonstrate that strong privacy guarantees in VFL federative systems may be fundamentally compromised.

This paper introduces *Intelligent City Defense*, a two-player zero-sum finite deterministic fully observable fully cooperative game involving resource management within SOA (Social Operational Adversarial Environment). In this simulation, one player acts as the city, defending against a multi-agent adversary targeting critical infrastructure like power and water systems via cyber attacks or physical sabotage. Each entity possesses unique capabilities for detection, response, movement, and attack/defense actions constrained by limited resources including fuel, battery, and charge limits that must be strategically allocated to maximize survival while minimizing damage scores. Both agents possess full knowledge of all visible and hidden information about each opponent's location, capabilities, and threat models. Starting with zero net infrastructure damage and tracking cumulative hits over time until no further moves remain, victory belongs to the player who survives with minimal cumulative damage once both sides are immobilized. We detail the architecture of an efficient multi-agent coordination algorithm designed to optimize resource distribution for persistent infrastructure protection. Furthermore, we present results from extensive trials against human players and existing AI benchmarks, demonstrating that our approach significantly outperforms baseline single-agent strategies while maintaining high computational efficiency.

This study examines how the dynamics of the Hawking–Page phase transition are influenced by variations in the mass of charged and scalar black holes confined within a cavity of a fixed volume. Specifically, we investigate how changes in either the charge parameter ($q$) or the scalar hair coupling constant ($\alpha$) affect transition temperatures and entropy at these transitions. Our findings indicate that increasing either $q$ or $\alpha$ consistently elevates the transition temperature and reduces the corresponding phase-change entropy gap. While such a reduction might superficially suggest a weakening of the phase transition, this conclusion is misleading because the magnitude of the reduction is outweighed by the associated dynamical effects. We further demonstrate that the nature of the Hawking–Page transition is driven by two competing mechanisms: one favoring small, short-lived horizons and another favoring large, long-lived ones. The relative dominance of these mechanisms shifts across different parameter regimes, ultimately dictating the transition's character.

Long-term, label noise persists in datasets, adversely affecting supervised learning by causing inaccurate predictions. Traditional approaches assume all samples within a single class are identical, ignoring potential variations among individual noisy instances of the same class, and often employ per-loss or smooth-loss functions to compute sample-level losses for efficient training. However, these methods calculate losses for every sample, resulting in high computational costs and inadequate handling of intra-class diversity to improve the ranking of documents within a specific label. To address this, the problem is addressed using a sampling strategy. Specifically, documents are sampled in groups. The method utilizes losses at the group level rather than at the individual instance level, and incorporates a graph-based model to effectively capture the similarity between query documents and those within each class. By integrating this graph-based model with group-level losses, a novel bag-loss function was developed for training. Empirical results indicate that this new loss function enhances inter-class margins, strengthens the internal consistency of classes, and is more efficient than calculating losses for every single instance. Additionally, incorporating this graph-based loss with labeling signals allows models to better rank similar query documents alongside other similar class members, thereby improving intra-class retrieval quality.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently achieved significant success across various domains involving labeled data points within graphs. To address common challenges, researchers have developed numerous techniques utilizing "pseudo labels" to train models more effectively. However, prior approaches often necessitate either extensive labeled data or rely on models already trained on vast labeled sets. This paper introduces "Info-P2," a novel algorithm designed to enhance performance in scenarios limited to very few labeled examples. By leveraging pseudo nodes and nodes situated in high information regions to guide training, Info-P2 creates initial pseudo labels that demonstrate greater node classification confidence compared to standard methods. Extensive testing across diverse graph classification benchmarks confirms Info-P2's ability to significantly surpass existing state-of-the-art approaches that also rely on pseudo labeling.

Beyond its experimental utility, this study provides a rigorous simulation framework for predicting betatron radiation in plasma environments for future analysis.

Differentially private distributed decision tree learning (DPTDTL) is a critical and rapidly emerging domain, yet current solutions are constrained by limitations in scalability, accuracy, or reliance on complex machine learning models that hinder interpretability. To address these gaps, we introduce a scalable and accurate framework capable of generating diverse tree structures. This framework offers multiple theoretical guarantees: first, it satisfies $\epsilon$-differential privacy with a strict upper bound on classification error; second, it includes data-dependent bounds on classification error and depth limited only by sufficient statistical information; and third, it incorporates stability guarantees for every component of the algorithmic chain. To further refine performance regarding accuracy, depth, and homogeneity, we develop two novel tree ensembles that integrate our methodological contributions with established machine learning techniques. Comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that this proposed framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art approaches in both accuracy and depth while incurring minimal privacy cost.

Although recent Hubble observations have bolstered the curvaton mechanism, the non-Gaussian component of primordial fluctuations remains unexplained within the framework. Headlines serve as concise and engaging summaries that frequently precede full articles, yet many online news services automatically generate these headlines using automated methods that often yield inferior results compared to manually created ones. Because automated headlines compromise the value of using summary as a metric to evaluate text generation models, distinguishing between human and automated news is critical. This study investigates the specific features and data conditions required to successfully identify automatically generated headlines. We analyze the impact of training data size on model performance and examine the advantages of models armed with visual access to the article. Our findings reveal that access to images enhances model performance, particularly with limited data; however, models can still accurately classify headline sources based on large datasets that lack image input. Finally, we demonstrate that models perform better when they perceive greater disparity in creating conditions between the human and automated groups. Ultimately, this work underscores the necessity of distinguishing automated headlines to uphold the validity of using headline generation as a benchmark for evaluating automated writing systems, thereby preventing models trained on mixed datasets from learning to replicate unwanted artificial characteristics.

In summary, our findings underscore the potential practical applications of non-crystalline configurations in exploring novel quantum states of matter.

Genuine Gamma Ray Blazars (FBLs) account for nearly half of the cases in Fermi-Lat detections spanning 100 MeV to 30 GeV, yet their spectral properties remain linked to several unidentified physical mechanisms. This study introduces a novel methodology for analyzing these spectra by utilizing a Bayesian neural network, which effectively categorizes the observed spectral behavior. We define two primary spectral behavior categories based on our spectral flux density models derived from the data. By employing a Bayesian neural network, we created a reliable classification system, enabling us to predict not only the most probable spectral behavior category for each observation but also the uncertainty associated with that prediction. Applying this framework to the entire catalog of extreme ultraviolet blazer detections (Fermi-Lat data up to 30 GeV), we identified two clusters in their spectral behavior distributions. For each cluster, we computed the predicted category alongside the associated confidence metric. The reliability of our approach is further validated by the fact that the spectral fits of 95% of the catalog entries remain within 90 percent a 90 degrees of the original spectral flux density measurements, with the remaining 5 percent attributable to either atypical spectral characteristics or stochastic noise.

Existing accessible-Web authoring tools primarily target desktop environments, leaving Web mobile social networking apps and platforms largely unsupported for creating accessible posts. This access gap stems from a lack of awareness among mobile social networking service (SNS) developers regarding accessibility. This paper outlines the current state of mobile social networking access and identifies obstacles and opportunities post-authoring, emphasizing the necessity for accessible mobile content creation. This approach involves integrating accessibility features directly into the user interface and experience. The paper concludes by setting the stage for designing and evaluating a mobile social media application that embeds assistive capabilities directly into its interface and user experience.

A hypergraph can be described as a set containing a graph and special edges called hyperedges, which consist of at least two vertices. A merge operation combines a hypergraph with a graph to create a larger hypergraph. In this study, the merge operation is generalized: it operates between a hypergraph and another hypergraph to produce a resulting hypergraph using set-theoretic constructions of their respective edge sets (or their hyper-graph representations as tensors, which are a type of set function). These set theoretic operations can be expressed as a merge operation on hyper-graph tensors, which represent the hyper-graph as a set of edges. These tensor merge operations include cases where a hyper-graph tensor is combined with an adjacency matrix of graph to form a hyper-graph tensor representing the union or intersection of their edges. Finally, the spectral properties associated with hyper-gon hyper-gone graph tensors resulting from tensor mergings in different ways are explored.

We are delighted to announce the successful selection of the Indian Spectroscopic and Imaging Space Telescope (INSIST) as the winner of the 2022 NASA Small Space Telescope Explorers Program Phase I study. INSIST is designed to deliver over 10 years of high-resolution spectroscopic and imaging data for the sky, with a specific emphasis on the galactic plane. This dataset will enable the creation of 3D maps of the nearby interstellar medium (ISM), facilitating a comprehensive understanding of the physical and chemical processes occurring within it. The telescope will employ a wide-field UV-optical imaging system and a multi-channel spectrograph, both equipped with wide bandwidth filters, to deliver observations unmatched in scope. This article provides a thorough overview of the science case driving the mission, along with a detailed description of the advanced instrumentation planned to achieve these scientific goals.

This study introduces a statistical technique utilizing natural cubic splines designed specifically for evaluating trials in Alzheimer's research, where patients receive daily treatments and exhibit fluctuating clinical metrics influenced by both long-term trends and short-term variability, alongside rising risks over time. While past analyses often assumed a strictly linear progression for the disease effect on outcomes, this approach replaces linearity with a flexible nonlinear spline structure defined by numerous potential parameters. We address this expansion by employing Bayesian regularization through spline smoothing priors selected via hyperparameter expansion, utilizing a leave-one-out cross-validation method to identify optimal regularization levels based on predictive accuracy for each spline. Empirical validation using simulated datasets with known parameters demonstrates that our expanded method maintains superior performance compared to traditional linear models, and the approach is further demonstrated through an analysis of a recent large-scale clinical trial in Alzheimer's research.

In nonequilibrium processes, the occurrence of an event is governed by an energy-like potential termed "action." While the method to find the event's duration-dependent action is established, a general approach to identify the most relevant transition paths is still missing. This study introduces a new algorithm that uses the action function as an input to optimize these dominant paths. The method's effectiveness in finding the most significant transitions is confirmed. Dominant paths represent the trajectories that minimize action over the full duration, yet they remain difficult to locate because this minimization is a highly complex, nonconvex problem. Furthermore, these paths are highly sensitive to the initial conditions selected from a random starting point. A key insight of this research is that one does not need to determine the entire dominant path to find a solution. Instead, an optimal subsegment starting or ending at a specific bifurcation point can yield the result. This approach proves highly effective because it allows that bifurcation point to serve as a constrained initial condition, significantly reducing both the difficulty and the search space compared to an unaided start.

This study addresses cross-domain, text-based SQL querying. To ensure effective generalization, we introduce a training strategy that integrates multiple auxiliary tasks designed to enhance both semantic interpretation and parameterization. Specifically, we developed a query context transformer to map a natural language statement into a query context vector, which then feeds into an analytical graph-based module to map elements of the language onto a database schema's query context. This language-independent graph-based mapping approach offers a robust framework for addressing various databases. In the auxiliary phase, we train this graph-based module using graph neural networks to predict features of query context vector predictions. Additionally, we train a predictor using node features and edge types to forecast connections between different components of a statement. Also, we train a predictor featuring a character-level CNN to convert input text keywords into word embeddings. Collectively, these measures help the network better understand key elements within a language statement. Experimental results indicate this model successfully identifies over 90% cross-domain SQL issues in terms of semantic interpretation and word matching, highlighting significant improvements.

An access structure is termed "intricate" when no accessible subset exists that can be formed by combining other accessible subsets. Intricacy functions as both an abductive measure and a theoretical framework for investigating access structures, holding value for both theoretical investigation and practical applications such as threshold cryptography. Notably, abductive reasoning itself—inferring likely premises from known conclusions—precludes deduction entirely; an intruder complexity in theory serves as an obstacle to establishing specific accessible subsets. Consequently, determining an arbitrary access structure's maximum size is NP-hard. Prior research by Birk and colleagues (2016) successfully resolved the optimal dimensions for universal access structures that are simultaneously intersection, uniform, and self dual. Building on this, this paper will present an optimal design for a specific non-uniform access structure type that fails to satisfy intersectionality or self-duality while meeting homogeneity requirements. Furthermore, this paper will provide closed form expressions for the maximum sizes of these previously studied structures under various axioms of symmetry. Finally, this research will highlight the potential of universal access structures that exhibit high levels of intricacy as valuable tools within threshold cryptography systems.

Continual learning focuses on training models incrementally across multiple tasks while preserving the ability to perform well on earlier ones without excessive memory demands. Although various methods have demonstrated promising results, this study serves as a practical, task-specific continual supervised learning baseline that aims to enable fair comparisons and drive future research. Surprisingly, this study reveals that a straightforward method utilizing pre-trained models is ineffective for this purpose. Instead, we found that a model trained from scratch on an extended sequence of tasks outperforms prototype methods that do not use pretrain. Our experiments show that this simple strategy achieves remarkable performance on mini-imageNet and ImageNet, reaching 65.1% and 70.0% accuracy respectively, while maintaining zero usage or training time on individual tasks to foster continued research into robust general continual learning methods.

We assess PAEP across three datasets—GigaNews, GigaSum, and XSum—demonstrating that it surpasses the extended baseline using multiple large-scale datasets. We observe that our method significantly boosts the performance metrics while enhancing the ability to generate grammatically correct sentences that follow summarization plans.

Furthermore, deriving the kinematic properties of the outflows will enhance our understanding of the physical mechanisms driving star formation suppression. To demonstrate the methodology, we present initial results from our early survey of dust emission and dense gas tracers in galaxy M82, a prominent starbursting galaxy.

Reinterpreting autonomous driving as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), we introduce a novel deep Q-network integrated with network pruning, designed to enhance the scalability of value function estimation. The parent network operates by cloning a prior optimal model and applying a gradient check to identify the best policy, while a subsequent optimization step fine-tunes new child models for improved performance compared to the parent. This iterative process continues until an optimal convergence point is reached. Experimental results indicate that this framework achieves superior learning efficiency and stability, producing policies with higher rewards and lower variance than traditional Q-learning methods.

Parallelization is a standard technique for multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs) to mitigate the evaluation time bias found in serial processing, which favors fast-evaluating candidates. This bias stems from asynchronous parallel MOEAs, a popular strategy that allows individual genomes to finish at different intervals due to varying computational demands. As this bias skews parent selection, it can severely degrade the quality of the final solution set. To address this issue, we introduce a new parallel algorithm that selects parents based on how often individuals appear in the population frequency. Our proposed algorithm eliminates evaluation time bias and was validated on the BENCH-VC benchmark suite using the 0/1-knapsack problem with time constraints. Our findings indicate that the fairness of the selection frequency approach is robust across all test instances.

However, high-resolution observations from our team successfully isolated the planetary signal from background noise. Further support comes from photometric data collected throughout the entire microlensing event, which precisely maps the ratio of planet-to-star mass projected into units of total system mass.

Linear open quantum systems lacking internal oscillations are widely understood and employed, largely due to the availability of robust analytical tools like the Magnus expansion and Litvinov series to model them. Conversely, practical applications often involve systems with intrinsic fast oscillations that lack efficient counterparts. However, the frequent presence of fast time oscillations inspired the development of the Floquet theory for unitary dynamics, though a specific theoretical framework has remained elusive. This gap is addressed by proposing the first mid-range theory—situated between exact methods like Floquet and fully perturbative approaches—designed for global many-body systems with fast time oscillations. The theory utilizes an averaging technique akin to multiple-scale analysis to treat a wide range of weakly open, oscillating non-autonomous systems. It assumes that oscillating terms and dissipation are comparable in magnitude, yielding a zeroth-order motion-free equation known as the effective Lindblad generator. The accuracy of the derived effective generator is validated against exact numerical results across a specific parameter regime. This methodology enables the application to diverse biological and technological contexts, such as optomechanics and photovoltaics, thereby facilitating model reduction for complex, oscillating systems and opening the way for novel quantum technologies.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become indispensable tools for machine learning on graph-structured data, yet their deployment faces hurdles such as high computational costs stemming from deep architectures, computational graph complexity, and non-linear operations, all alongside challenges in hyperparameter optimization. To address these issues, we introduce `gpune`, a highly optimized GNN framework parameterized for automatic tuning of training hyperparameters and computational configurations to meet specific hardware requirements. This tool enables users to swiftly test multiple model and hardware variations to identify the optimal setup for a given task and resource constraint. Comprehensive experiments on various graphs processing GNNs across different machines demonstrate that our tool offers superior plotting of performance landscapes compared to existing methodologies and delivers up to 2.2× faster execution than state-of-the-art frameworks.

The Legendre Memory Network Block (LMB) serves as a key component in the PLeND architecture by integrating solid-state drive (SSD) flash memory with deep learning. Traditionally, LMB training involves sequential updates to the memory bank, creating significant time delays and underutilizing the parallel processing potential of GPUs. This work redefines the LMB training algorithm to enable this shift, thereby reducing execution duration and fully leveraging GPU capabilities. We also present an optimized, memory-efficient implementation that avoids expensive operations such as matrix multiplications and matrix additions while handling data layout for maximum performance gains. This approach delivers up to 2.5x performance improvements over the serial method and matches or surpasses CPU handling speed, all while requiring a 30% reduction in memory footprint compared to existing parallel solutions.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a robust method for addressing multifidelity problems by integrating multi-source data within a unified optimization framework. Canopus is a highly performant distributed consensus protocol with the ability to scale up. We introduce RCanopus, a new system derived from it that provides stronger safety guarantees by accommodating client failures and handling Byzantine faults among servers, while scaling horizontally to address these complexities. While earlier high-throughput consensus protocols typically relied on the assumption of server fault tolerance, RCanopus shifts the paradigm by only requiring a quorum of servers to be correct in order to guarantee client state consistency, thereby accepting state divergence among server nodes as a reality. We further address network churn, a frequent occurrence in massive-scale distributed environments, and mitigate the "computation of work wasted problem" that arises when a client repeatedly re-executes identical requests following a server failure. Finally, RCanopus is positioned as a robust foundation for next-generation, scalable distributed databases and storage solutions.

Recent advancements in deep object detection have produced models that are highly precise yet often lack confidence and uncertainty metrics essential for real-world deployments. This paper introduces BayesOD, a framework designed to estimate uncertainty for object detection neural networks without compromising training speed, inference accuracy, or confidence scores. Leveraging uncertainty propagation analysis, BayesOD trains a post-processing network trained on the first moments of object detection predictions' posterior distributions, coupled with an efficiency metric derived from second moments. Benchmark tests on COCO datasets reveal significant improvements over existing uncertainty estimation techniques; the model reduces prediction error by 12% and enhances mean IOU uncertainty estimation accuracy by 16%.

Accurate forecasting of traffic density is vital for effective congestion management. Existing deep learning methods typically address this by forecasting future states across complete road maps, frequently beginning the calculation process after detecting current congestion. However, traffic conditions evolve rapidly, rendering past-based predictions relatively slow. To overcome these constraints, this paper proposes an innovative methodology leveraging "traffic moving snippets"—dynamic sub-sections of video traffic footage as fundamental features, alongside novel deep neural networks to forecast future states of these snippets. Consequently, a specific network module is designed solely to localize and extract traffic segments from video frames. Furthermore, a second network component predicts the subsequent state of a snippet given its history. Experimental evaluations against a baseline method demonstrate that our approach not only outperforms standard models but also executes the prediction significantly faster than the baseline.

This research reports on the outcomes of a Monte Carlo simulation examining the influence of cosmic rays on particles trapped within the low Earth orbit (LEO) radiation belt. We specifically analyzed trajectories for incident particles with energies of 100 MeV across three types—protons, deuterons, and alpha particles. Results indicate that cosmic ray particles are scattered throughout LEO, leading to energy degradation where the original incident particles transform into secondary particles that remain confined within the LEO radiation belt. These findings broaden the scope of radiation effect studies concerning trapped particles in LEO. Additionally, we observed that the average energy of the resulting secondary particles closely matches the energy required for an electron to undergo ionization, suggesting these secondary particles are the primary contributors to radiation damage to spacecraft within the LEO radiation belt.

Experiments on diverse synthetic tasks demonstrate that the operator can precisely manage minor and major modifications in graphs with high fidelity. Finally, we apply the framework to the real-world domains of brain lesion segmentation and brain tumor grading, yielding promising initial results.

Astronomers currently lack a universally accepted model for the properties of interstellar dust, particularly in regions sparsely populated with it. This gap hampers our ability to analyze extinction curves, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) spectra, and linearly polarized thermal emission effectively. To resolve this issue, we have created the Astrodust+PAH Model, which offers a physically grounded and comprehensively polarizable framework. This model provides a unified explanation for the extinction of interstellar light and its subsequent re-emission across the near-infrared to far-infrared spectrum, including polarization signals. Grounded in observations, the model utilizes three key parameters: the size of core dust silicates (ranging from 0.100.150.1μ), their fractional abundance, and the number of electrons on each PAH. By incorporating these variables, we can synthesize complex spectral signatures from single, physically motivated inputs. Furthermore, by varying dust morphology and size in the context of our polarizable formalism, we successfully reproduce the observed interstellar polarization patterns. Ultimately, this model establishes a standardized, polar-sensitive method for characterizing dust composition in diverse environments, ranging from the sparse interstellar medium to dense molecular clouds.

Abstract Interpretation constitutes a framework for finding approximated solutions to program analysis problems. By mapping exact solutions—often theoretically undecidable—to a more permissive, dense representation of descent operators, this field makes such computations tractable while balancing precision against efficiency through careful selection. Historically, however, there has been no systematic method for mitigating accuracy loss, with the only available strategy being the iterative refinement of operators. Despite the widespread adoption of operator decoupling in compiler implementations, particularly within the construction of control flow graphs where computation proceeds separately for each node using post-order traversal, this technique has remained underutilized in abstract interpretation itself. This paper addresses that gap by introducing a new decoupling framework that isolates operator components responsible for handling rising versus descending computations. Specifically, we show that the descent operator's infinite hierarchy can be approximated by pairing functions, with each component processed independently per edge in a graph structure. This modularization enables the application of distinct precision-efficiency trade-offs to rising functions (independent of input) and descent functions (dependent on input values). We further present an optimized implementation utilizing parallel processing and provide a numerical analysis demonstrating that this method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art approaches.

Phonon topology has become a rapidly expanding field, yielding both fundamental insights and promising pathways for emerging technologies. This study investigates how optical pumping influences the topological order of phonons in perovskites. Using molecular dynamics simulations, we examine the topological insulator BaTiO$_3$ under intense laser excitation. The results reveal that strong pumping can alter the system's global topology, a phenomenon explained by the reduction in effective masses and hopping amplitudes within the band structure alongside a significant shift in phonon-phonon scattering rates. Consequently, this research demonstrates a pathway to accessing novel topological phases and non-equilibrium topological phonon states through optical control.

Outlier detection is a fundamental challenge in data mining that typically relies on graph-based structures like k-nearest neighbor (k-NN) graphs to balance detection speed and accuracy. However, the novel approach presented here employs super-radiant (SR) graphs to achieve both exact outlier detection and significantly lower computational costs. By relaxing the rigid constraints of conventional k-NN graphs, SR-graphs facilitate the creation of more uniform super-neighbor structures capable of guiding searches more precisely. Furthermore, these dynamic structures support efficient maintenance when new data points are introduced. Experimental evaluations on various test datasets demonstrate that the proposed strategy surpasses traditional baselines, delivering comparable or superior results with markedly reduced processing times.

This study introduces the concept of community fairness based on a graph structure. We define this fairness as the requirement that localized communities exhibit similar outcomes regarding a target attribute. We further establish that achieving such fairness may necessitate re-assigning nodes to form a new set of communities. Consequently, our objective is to develop general machine learning models on graphs capable of evaluating community fairness regarding specific traits, using the first framework to ensure equitable distribution of these traits. We propose a Bayesian framework within this first model to quantify fairness by measuring the probability that an attribute falls within predefined bounds per community. The computational challenges posed by this framework, which involves intractable integrations, are resolved to enable practical implementation on any graph. We demonstrate the utility of our techniques by assessing fairness of gender attribution between graphic networks representing professional affiliations and academic collaborations. The results of this analysis, coupled with fair-aware graph learning, facilitate bias mitigation in network analysis through a combination of traditional statistical adjustments and re-assigning units to re-define communities as necessary.

This paper demonstrates that reversible kinetic mechanisms can be approximated iteratively by applying linear steady-state analysis to specific scenarios where a single parameter approaches zero or infinity. This approach was examined using two reversible models with multiple substrates, beginning with a random-order mechanism and moving to a sequential sequence involving a ternary complex. Each iteration refines the kinetic constant estimation by calculating the dimensionless initial reaction velocity relative to the theoretical maximum, subsequently updating the reaction parameter and repeating calculations until convergence results match exact solutions. Foundational iterations yield approximations consistent with Haldane's relationship but constrained by its structural constraints, whereas secondary iterations recover the full relationship linking enzyme turnover, initial velocity, and substrate concentrations. Consequently, these iterative methods serve to numerically resolve irreversible enzyme kinetics while offering numerical insights into reversible catalytic processes.

This work introduces a new architecture for local feature description and matching designed to be independent of keypoint detection mechanisms. Unlike most existing models relying on convolutional neural networks (CNNs)—which struggle with extreme scales or high-resolution images when features are distant or small—LoFTR leverages self-exceptive transformers to establish correspondences efficiently even under such challenging geometric conditions. Specifically, our approach extracts local descriptors directly from image pairs by learning cross-correlation at the correspondence level through a multi-head mechanism tailored for matching remote features. We further refine the resulting binary or soft correspondences via a soft non-maximum suppression strategy. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that LoFTR achieves superior accuracy relative to CNN-based state-of-the-art local feature methods when handling disjoint features characterized by wide baselines or low feature density.

Inferring vector magnetic field data for the Sun is becoming a common approach, driven by the growing availability of observations from facilities lacking full polarization sensitivity. However, these inference methods rely on prior distributions that introduce an inherent risk of biases being embedded directly into the results. Standard practice typically employs SVD-based linear inversions to merge polarized light measurements with prior information under the assumption of a Gaussian model, thereby implicitly anchoring outcomes to specific prior means. Consequently, many studies inadvertently introduce biases into their inferred measurements, often failing to identify the sources of these anomalies. This work presents a general framework for detecting prior-induced biases in inferred measurements and outlines strategies to refine specific datasets. Using observations from the DKIST instrument, we evaluated linear and nonlinear SVD inversion methods alongside a new nonlinear Bayesian inversion method. Our analysis reveals that both linear and nonlinear SVD inversion methods produce significant biases in key differentiating parameters, such as the magnitude of line-of-sight magnetism, specifically manifesting an average bias of roughly 15%. In contrast, the nonlinear Bayesian inversion fails to exhibit such biases. We further examine different refinement tactics to mitigate these issues, including techniques that relax constraints on specific data points while preserving overall smoothness without the biases inherent to the original model. Our findings indicate that both approaches effectively reduce biases in most scenarios. Ultimately, these techniques are versatile and applicable to a broad range of SVD inversion methods.

Demand Side Management (DSM) represents a vital element within modern energy grids. While traditional models utilize economic incentives—such as dynamic electricity tariffs—to guide consumer rational choices for lower costs and improved energy efficiency, the rise of smart homes equipped with Internet of Things (IoT) devices offers new avenues. These networks enable inter-device communication, facilitating coordinated energy scheduling that is critical given limited supply capacity. However, since consumers prefer real-time pricing over predetermined rates, and since actual price costs are revealed only after energy usage, we introduce an innovative DSM framework leveraging implicit pricing driven by dynamic energy billing rates. Guided by these dynamic rates, IoT devices autonomously optimize their tasks to maximize utility within supply constraints, engaging in strategic interactions that are mathematically modeled as an aggregative game to ensure decentralized equilibrium and stability under shortages. Simulations involving an IoT ecosystem, including a smart meter, thermostat, and washing machine, demonstrate superior performance of our approach compared to both random scheduling and static tariff systems.

The Gaia Blue-Photometry and Red-Photorometer (BP/RP) spectra have already identified numerous hypergiars and asymptotic giant branch stars. This study introduces an automated method to detect metal-poor main sequence stars within these data, utilizing a technique inspired by independent analyses of Gaia G-BP and G-RP luminosity function. By segmenting the spectra into gaps and mapping their average intensity against metallicity calibration curves for those specific regions, we successfully flag candidate metal-poor objects. Additionally, a verification process filters these selections against observed spectra, utilizing known metallicity indicators to confirm the results. Testing this approach yielded 1,200 candidate stars down to a metallicity of $[Fe/H] = -3.5$ from a total $G$-band sample of 11 million, with the candidates comprising 1.1%. We further provide examples of four confirmed low-metallicity stars, with three of them having spectroscopic measurements of $[Fe/H] < -2.5$. Finally, our findings demonstrate that these rare stars follow a consistent metallicity distribution, despite comprising only 0.11% of the total population.

Risk parity is a critical challenge in algorithmic trading across various sectors, particularly algorithmic advertising, where advertisers aim to maximize campaign impact by selecting optimal bids. Despite this shared objective, real-world complexities create significant hurdles. Research into risk parity specifically for display algorithmic advertising remains limited, and current methods often rely on costly and impractical approaches. This paper introduces an innovative budget-aware trading method that is both cost-effective and effective at managing risk parity. The proposed solution leverages Reinforcement Learning (RL) to develop adaptive strategies that dynamically balance risk parity and budget utilization. Additionally, a unique bidding regulation mechanism is employed to further ensure stability and predictability in algorithmic trading operations. The method was rigorously evaluated against real-world datasets from a major display advertising firm operating online platforms; both simulation results and real-world tests demonstrate its superiority over established benchmarks such as traditional fixed-rate methods and benchmark RL algorithms capable of autonomously learning strategies without strict risk parity constraints.

A central inquiry driving quantum optics is whether the Wigner function serves as a reliable model for light across all physical contexts. We demonstrate that answers to this pivotal question hinge on whether quantum guidance formalism is universally valid; specifically, the nature of Wigner function behavior in continuum quantum field theories mirrors negative eigenvalues in the Wilson loop, which act as obstructions to the quantum guidance principle. Consequently, by leveraging non-eigen-Wilson scenarios to non-eigen-photon systems exhibiting negative Wigner values, we provide an alternative perspective on Wigner function limitations, while the derivation of a positivity theorem for the Wigner function in discrete systems using antisymmetric states offers new insights into spin systems like Bose-Hubbub and lattice models. Thus, our discussion addresses both historical and contemporary inquiries regarding the physical significance of the Wigner function.

This work examines the security of privacy amplification within a general class of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols that rely on non-uniform random seeds. We establish a framework to analyze the approximate min-entropy of an arbitrary source conditioned on system states and subsequently derive an analytical formula for the entropy of a uniformly distributed source. This formula applies to any finite correlation regarding the system states and the conditional data source, alongside associated data processing inequalities. These results offer practical value for the security verification of QKD protocols utilizing arbitrary random seeds and states that may be partially correlated or entangled with an adversary's systems. The proposed approach is further demonstrated through limit analysis of the 1-integrated phase scheme with one-way error correction and conditional error correction.

This article examines two distinct classes of timelike Bertrand curves, specifically offset and isotropic ones, within a Friedmann-Lemaître-Weinberg space-like (FLWs), which is modeled as a pseudo-Riemannian manifold of index 2. We demonstrate that every timelike closed curve belongs to one of these two categories by analyzing isotropic and offset properties and presenting several examples to further illustrate these results.

We propose an advanced extension of the Dyson-based framework for analyzing spontaneous scattering between highly excited Rydberg atoms situated within waveguides, under conditions of weak inter-atom coupling. Our key innovation allows for the systematic calculation of multi-photon scattering amplitudes arising from arbitrary orders of perturbation theory, with higher-particle processes captured through closed-form analytical expressions and associated combinatorial coefficients. The core of our approach is a graph-based, easy-to-implement method that effectively incorporates interactions up to any desired level of precision. Additionally, we validate the accuracy of this scheme through comparisons with exact exact-diagonalization numerical simulations to establish its utility for analyzing Rydberg scattering in waveguide quantum electrodynamics systems.

Non-coherent differential detection of constant composition code (CCP) modulation enhances robustness in multipath fading and signal attenuation environments, such as those caused by attenuation or multipath effects. Time-efficient reward learning (TERL) addresses the challenge of defining task rewards efficiently without excessive human input. This study introduces VRACD, a novel method employing visual ranking within gathered data clusters to acquire quick and accurate feedback. The approach involves generating multiple sets of samples via a large language model (LLM) and prompting it to create descriptive task sentences that act as non-termed rewards for various models; subsequently, humans perform fewest visual inspections to select the best set, serving as selected positive examples and negative samples. Two primary mechanisms for generating these descriptive tasks are examined: direct prompt-based extraction from the LLM or a few-shot setup utilizing task sentences previously chosen by a human operator. The paper further details a visual cluster-based interface allowing a user to evaluate multiple algorithmic proposals simultaneously and manually adjust selections. Additionally, we developed an algorithm optimizing the sequence of questions to maximize the information gained from each interaction step. Empirical evidence supports VRACD as an effective TERL technique, capable of generating high-quality data for diverse tasks and reducing the count of visual checks needed in scenarios with human-in-the-loop constraints.

NGC 2808 serves as a representative blue-straggler dominated globular cluster, characterized by a significant spread in turnoff (TO) masses. This phenomenon is widely linked to non-standard stellar evolution, specifically mass transfer, and its formation is believed to be influenced by the initial mass function (IMF) and initial metallicities of the most massive stars. To resolve these constraints, we conducted a high-precision study of Mg I lines within blue turnoff stars, yielding an abundance ratio of [Mg/Fe] = +0.37 ± 0.07 derived from a sample size of 12 stars. This analysis reveals a robust correlation between [Mg/Fe] variations and stellar mass ($M_{\star}$), characterized by a slope of $-0.2 \pm 0.1$. Consequently, we report a total metallicity spread of $\Delta$[Mg/Fe] = 0.24 ± 0.08 across the cluster's most massive stars, confirming previous reports that indicate a spread of $\Delta$[Mg/Fe] = 0.18. Furthermore, observations of He-variability in horizontal branch stars suggest that helium spreads follow a trend similar to metallicity spreads. Under the assumption that He spreads mimic metallicity spreads, NGC 2808 exhibits an exceptionally high $\Delta$(Y/Ze) value of 0.30 ± 0.

Furthermore, our analysis proves that performing quantum operations—applying a post-measurement operator alongside square-root weights corresponding to two different observables—is mathematically equivalent to applying the corresponding Bayes' rule for the associated quantum inferences. In the process, the authors also establish the consistency requirements for quantum measurements regarding state transformations.

Ultraviolet (UV) emission lines in the UV range serve as potent tracers for cosmic structures, ranging from individual objects to vast clusters. Among these, the Lyman-alpha filter offers a powerful tool for detecting hydrogen within high-redshift galaxies at a distance where the radiation is redshifted. However, achieving a sufficiently narrow bandwidth for Lyman-alpha filters proves technically difficult due to the inherent limits of optical components. To overcome obstacles in detecting high-redshift galaxies, our team has developed a specialized L-alpha filter designed for telescopes like the Large Binocular Telescope. Our results indicate that this new device attains exceptional performance, achieving an out-of-band extinction of greater than OD 4, while maintaining an ultra-narrow passband of 0.165 ± 0.002 nm centered precisely at the target wavelength.

This study introduces a graph symmetric distributed method for addressing optimal management issues within systems of symmetrical nonlinear time-varying dynamics. This approach leverages properties of graph partitioning and utilizes graph filters to enable the optimization process in these systems. Specifically, graph partitioning is exploited to facilitate the distribution of tasks, while graph filters aid in solving them via a distributed strategy. Consequently, each agent can locally derive its optimized partition and associated coefficients, learning the global filter weights, and determining global management parameters independently. Validated through a case study involving traffic flow optimization on a road network, the work demonstrates results that remain unaffected by communication delays, random data packet loss, and irregular patterns of dropouts.

Web environments host billions of images, most of which remain inaccessible due to a lack of organized indexing. As opposed to these being static, the maintenance of web graphics is dynamic and often involves automatic adjustments to properties like scaling and colorization. Consequently, a new methodology for a dynamic indexing strategy is required to effectively manage these constant changes in scale and appearance. This study proposes such a method by introducing a technique that leverages color histograms across diverse resizing levels to maintain efficient operations for image retrieval and searching. Experimental results indicate that this approach outperforms existing methodologies.

Keyless Physical Layer Security (PLS) represents a promising approach to secure communications, leveraging channel characteristics to enable pairs of nodes to establish a shared, third-party-secret key. While research on PLS has largely concentrated on deterministic channel models like TDD wireless communications and wired networks, minimal attention has been paid to scenarios involving channel fluctuation models like AWGN. This paper introduces Keyless Verification for AWGN (VKCV) channels, offering a method to audit randomness extraction that previously lacked a formal framework. We provide VKCV channel capacity formulas and a set of necessary and sufficient conditions. Additionally, VKCV encompasses a broad range of practical channel types, underscoring the importance of the study for real-world applications of PLS.

This study examines the behavior of a charged particle trapped in an electrical potential subject to white noise thermal fluctuations, with the potential shape modulated in a "washboard" pattern by a periodic function. We establish conditions under which the long-term dynamics approximate a simple drift-and-diffusion equation via a refined Taylor expansion of the non-linear Hamiltonian system. By deriving explicit formulas for the drift velocity and effective diffusivity based on these expansions, we demonstrate why previous experimental observations indicated near-zero displacement velocity in such systems under specific conditions.

This study addresses the challenge of quantifying market responses to surprise announcements using standard high-frequency financial data. A key difficulty lies in accurately pinpointing the moment an announcement becomes known, a task often complicated by the simultaneous release of data in real-time. Existing threshold change-detection techniques can mislead when the speed of market information release vastly exceeds the speed of actual announcement release. Our approach leverages the local projection method to estimate impulse reactions, accommodating a wide array of potential event timing models directly within the reaction function. This reaction function is then optimized using change detection solely on pre-announcement volatility patterns. Our method's advantages are demonstrated through robust performance against standard high-frequency techniques in simulated environments. Finally, when applied to a portfolio of over 200 microstructure event stocks, we find strong evidence that accurately detecting the event timing critically influences both the accuracy of inferring reaction patterns and the efficacy of capturing momentum.

This study investigates the rotational force, known as the Angulo Casimir Torque, acting upon a charged Dirichlet plate situated within another parallel plate in a quantum vacuum. By employing a model where an external magnetic field quantizes the plate's electronic energy levels into Landau levels, and a charge experiences a logarithmic radial potential, the authors analyze the torque exerted on an isolated charge near such surfaces. Their analysis reveals that within quantized energy structures like Landau levels, the torque exhibits pronounced non-monotonic behavior characterized by sharp peaks and troughs. These findings suggest that manipulating the position and dynamics of nuclear matter could enable the control of Casimir-torqued rotation. Specifically, if implemented, this phenomenon could enhance our understanding of quantum vacuum interactions and open new frontiers for manipulating nuclear states through purely quantum electrodynamic forces.

Fine-grained named entity recognition (FG-NEC) requires distinguishing among various entity types for the same organization, geographic region, or person. While existing work often trains BERT-based transformers using hyperbolic space embeddings to encode fine-grained features, we propose RFNET-RH, a linear-space method that effectively leverages established hyperbolic geometric representations. By combining these embeddings with traditional bi-LSTM-based bi-directional encoding and specialized attention mechanisms, we adapt these models to standard embedding spaces. We demonstrate competitive or superior performance across multiple benchmarks, achieving top results on two out of the six tested datasets in seven instances. Our analysis confirms that hyperbolic embeddings successfully capture nuanced information and that a multi-dimension attention strategy effectively balances contextual data derived from diverse linguistic features.

Specifically, we transform the original estimation problem into an equivalent finite support constrained problem, resolving it through multiple parallel sub-optimizations over a limited time window. Document summarization, a well-established yet enduring research domain, has historically focused heavily on the English language. This paper introduces GAE-ISumm, an unsupervised, neural, algebraic-free, end-to-end framework designed to generate key-based summaries for Indian languages. Specifically, the model creates succinct canonical keys through a graph-based framework utilizing the EA-GNN architecture and subsequently decodes meaningful content from these keys. Furthermore, this study presents the Hindi SummCorpus, a new standard benchmark for machine summarization targeting Indian languages, which consists of 1000 pairs for Hindi (data from the Wikipedia corpus) and 1000 pairs for Tamil (data from the Google Translate API). Evaluating the model on these corpus collections, GAE-ISumm achieves significant performance, surpassing state-of-the-art English-based approaches by approximately 10% across the Hindi and Tamil language pairs.
