Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have become a cornerstone of Bayesian deep learning by uniting deep learning capabilities with variational inference. The standard VAE framework comprises an encoder that approximates the true posterior of latent variables and a generative model acting as the exact prior, with training driven by the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO). Lately, regularized VAEs have emerged to enhance reconstruction fidelity and address scalability issues inherent in ELBO maximization by re-casting the objective as solving a latent variable system under fixed generative parameters. This paper introduces an extension where VAEs employ regularized fixed-point algorithms to achieve faster and more stable convergence. We further demonstrate that, utilizing fixed generative parameters, the proposed objective yields a superior likelihood estimate compared to the ELBO. Empirical results on the MNIST dataset confirm that this regularized VAE produces tighter posterior distributions and markedly improves reconstruction quality.

The increasing popularity of intelligent household devices has concurrently elevated the risks regarding data privacy, user information confidentiality, and the integrity of the automated control systems themselves. At the core of this issue is a critical gap: many contemporary smart gadgets lack the capacity to securely transmit data, necessitating robust local monitoring mechanisms to address privacy flaws and hardware malfunctions. Decentralized private blockchains are well-suited to mitigate these challenges by offering decentralized data storage, immutable record-keeping, and enhanced transparency to trusted stakeholders. This study introduces an innovative framework designed for a local area network environment, enabling robust blockchain-supported tracking of household gadgets; this system utilizes low-cost positioning devices for geographic localization of smart components and internet-of-things (IoT) technology for direct data acquisition. Furthermore, it outlines comprehensive methodologies for positioning verification and data processing to validate the proposed architecture and its effectiveness.

A new architecture named L-Quantizer has been developed for this purpose. A significant innovation of our approach is the capability to handle gray-coded mappings, which were previously unsupported in state-of-the-art learning systems for the same task. To the authors' knowledge, this represents the initial integration of these learning systems with such encodings in prior research. A particularly valuable attribute of the proposed design is its compatibility across multiple code types, including the ability to scale for new applications easily without redesign.

Domain Adaption (DA) is designed to enhance model performance when labeled data is absent in the target domain. Traditionally, DA relies on data re-collection by combining source and target data to compute posterior probabilities via a Bayesian framework, selecting the highest probability class as the label. However, this hypothesis shift strategy suffers from performance limitations due to noisy predictions. To address this, we introduce a semi-supervised approach optimized for source-hypothesis alignment. Our solution involves leveraging the ensemble of predictions from a teacher network trained on both labeled and artificially augmented target data. To further strengthen model robustness, we integrate a cross-entropic loss function within the framework. Furthermore, to leverage both cross-domain feature alignment and local consistency within the target domain, we employ a cross-domain supervised classification objective alongside a target domain self-labeling mechanism to supervise the subsequent semi-supervised stages effectively. Experimental evaluations across benchmark datasets demonstrate that this semi-supervised paradigm achieves state-of-the-art results.

We introduce a deterministic algorithm designed to guide Reservoir Computing networks to learn temporal sequences, eliminating the need for backpropagation-based training of their internal connections. This paper investigates whether the recurrent dynamics observed in high-performing deep learning models arise from their architecture or from the problem domains in which they are deployed. To address this question, we modified our partially observable partially irreversible (POIri) environment framework, previously introduced by \cite{vanHaaften2019}, allowing us to train agents based explicitly on their last, second-to-last, or third-to-last actions. Planetary migration can establish close approaches between planets moving at similar speeds within their progenitor disk. The primary mechanism driving this shift is the depletion of disk mass due to accretion, which concurrently alters the positions of critical points in disks of $4\times10^{25}\,g\,cm^{-2}$ and modifies the torque balance. Carbon-based nanomaterials hold promise for creating compact solid-state electronics and energy systems due to their vast variety of electronic and transport properties. This study examines how temperature and gate voltage affect the resistance of an armchair single-walled carbon nanotube (SWCNT) film. At low temperatures, we observed a shift from phonon-dominated behavior at high bias to activation transport at low bias. By modeling this activation transport alongside a series combination of contacts and barriers, combined with analysis of low-temperature oscillations driven by electrostatic filling factors, we determined that transport is governed by phonon-assisted tunneling. Furthermore, transport energy gaps correlate with the calculated band structures of armchair SWCNTs possessing specific chiral indices. These findings underscore the critical role of phonons in electronic transport across low-dimensional and disordered conductors.

Fuzzy clustering remains a popular technique for analyzing research data because it can distinguish datasets into multiple classes and determine cluster affiliations, which is not always possible with traditional clustering. However, early versions like Fuzzy k-means are limited to handling only low-dimensional data. This paper addresses this gap by proposing an enhanced FkWmeans methodology that optimizes feature weights based on inter-class entropy to deliver superior clustering outcomes. To evaluate the performance of these proposed approaches, an original metric for inter-class entropy was formulated. The performance of the new methods was validated through extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating that minimizing inter-class entropy leads to improved results. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to tackle feature weight optimization in high and very high dimensionality contexts using entropy-driven strategies.

Evade attacks serve as a significant threat to the Android operating system by enabling malicious apps to bypass OS-level security mechanisms designed to restrict their privileged access. Consequently, evading attacks have catalyzed widespread research and led to numerous detection methodologies that analyze app behavior across multiple layers to identify existing compromises. Despite advancements in detection, the broader community lacks a comprehensive understanding regarding how these attacks issue-specificly function and vary across different OS components. To address this gap, this study conducts an exhaustive review of the literature concerning Android evasions to establish a holistic perspective on their landscape. We categorize these threats according to the specific OS components they target and present an initial categorization framework categorizing evasion strategies into three non-mutually exclusive issue areas: (1) Issue-space evasion attacks targeting individual OS components directly, (2) Operational-space evasion attacks circumventing the OS through indirect pathways, and (3) Operational-time evasion attacks exploiting temporal loopholes. A detailed examination follows for each issue-area regarding their characteristics, alongside a comprehensive survey of relevant literature within those frameworks drawn from over 1,000 empirical studies.

Nuclear short-range correlations (SRCs) are defined as high-momentum states that emerge with relatively low probability (~5-10%) in nuclear wavefunctions. Furthermore, we employ a simplified model framework based on plane-wave inputs to derive a closed-form expression involving Fourier transforms, which connects this density operator to measurable quantities like nuclear structure functions via a space-time framework grounded in the Wigner function formalism applied to nuclear many-body systems. Investigating complex-valued equalities is essential for the foundational stability of theoretical deep learning. To resolve this, this paper introduces a set of solutions centered around *correlation* to establish a unified theory complex-valued deep learning. Specifically, we define a correlation function that maps two complex numbers into real values, thereby eliminating issues related to non-existence, non-uniqueness, non-continuity, and non-computability linked to complex function equality. Consequently, this enables complex-valued deep learning models to remain numerically stable throughout their existence, non-unique cases, non-continuous operations, and computationally feasible computations. These findings establish a new branch within neural network research focused on solving complex numbers via correlation. Numerical experiments confirm our approach yields stable outcomes by accurately modeling complex numbers—demonstrated here through stable out-of-class detection—while maintaining a concise formulation and minimal computational overhead.

Clustering is a critical element in managing disease spread, yet identifying meaningful clusters remains a significant challenge. This issue is particularly acute in the context of outbreaks governed by specific networks, such as those defined by proximity, contact patterns, or social structures. This study investigates the asymptotic behavior of clusters as the population expands. By modeling a cluster as a function of the network's structure and the mechanism generating cases, we characterize its size and distribution using geometric principles. Specifically, we demonstrate that cluster sizes follow a Poisson process, while the size distribution of clusters with positive occurrences is governed by a power law whose exponent is determined by the network's dimensionality. These findings offer insights into effective strategies for disease suppression through targeted geometric interventions.

This study develops a strategy for estimating indirect effects in causal models where an exposure, a mediator, and an outcome are linked sequentially, specifically utilizing sampling methods drawn from causal inference and biostatistics. Using either simple random or stratified random cases-control designs, the proposed approach estimates the impact of an intervention that affects both an intermediate mediator and final outcome. It also provides estimators for direct effects. Applications span scenarios such as assessing how dietary vitamin intake influences blood levels and subsequent cancer risk, or how exercise affects cholesterol levels and heart attack likelihood. Notably, the study demonstrates that average treatment effect estimation from these cases-controllers matches that achieved through full population data analysis. Simulation findings indicate that our efficiently selected estimators outperform existing fully analyzed methods found in the literature when dealing with cases-controllers, offering greater precision.

This study explores secure transmission strategies for Reflective Intelligent Surface (RIS)-assisted wireless systems, accounting for hardware impairments. Specifically, it addresses two scenarios: (a) cases where both the legitimate user (SU) and RIS suffer from impairments, and (b) cases involving only one hardware impairment between SU and RIS. The objective is to simultaneously maximize secrecy capacity while ensuring full connectivity for both user pairs. To achieve this, we develop a low-complexity algorithm based on Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). Simulation outcomes indicate that the proposed method can achieve near-optimal secrecy rates with minimal computational complexity. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that secrecy rates increase as hardware impairment levels decrease. Additionally, the analysis reveals that maintaining SU-U connectivity necessitates ensuring that the RIS-user pair establishes a direct line-of-sight path.

Specifically, through hindsight summarization, we allow a master model to evaluate the alignment and quality of predictions issued by a sub-model. Using these evaluations, a simple policy gradient algorithm trains the curator to sample more meaningful training examples and generate corrections for erroneous ones. Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, millisecond-duration flashes of high-frequency radio waves whose origins remain largely unexplained, despite their detection being established in recent years. While strong support exists for a compact extragalactic origin, specifically involving young massive stellar populations, relativistic jets, or supermassive black hole systems, the physical mechanisms behind them are still debated. Research has been conducted to determine the constraints of extragalactic distances and the sizes of these emitting regions by analyzing simultaneous and delayed optical emissions from FRBs. Utilizing Swift's UVOT and ground-based instruments, we searched for visible light signals from seven well-defined bursts identified in the data. Our study found no confirmed simultaneous or delayed optical events; specifically, searches for simultaneous emission yielded null results at levels exceeding 100 times above background noise across the $U_V$ band. Furthermore, we looked specifically for visible light coincident within $\pm 100$ ms before and after the radio bursts, also finding nothing. Our upper limits on total energy show constraints greater than $10^{39}$–$10^{40}$ ergs for simultaneous emission bursts and $10^{37}$ ergs for delayed emission bursts. Consequently, these findings rule out small pre-explosion regions smaller than $10^{13}$–$10^{14}$ cm.

Step sampling algorithms have become a standard method for calculating free energy landscapes and partition functions for systems involving many variables. Significant progress has recently focused on systems constrained by fixed values of an order parameter. While these fixes aid in mapping free energy landscapes, the resulting nested sampling algorithms lack fully developed methods for handling these constraints. This study examines three specific approaches to handle ordered constrained parameters within the context of step sampling and evaluates their performance. Using the Ising model, a binary mixture, and a binary ion system as test cases, the free energy landscapes generated by each technique are compared and analyzed. Results indicate that the algorithm's performance varies depending entirely on the chosen method and on how sharply the free energy minimum corresponds to fixed order parameter values. Furthermore, it is noted that two of the three step sampling variants fail to converge due to a specific technical defect.

We introduce the fault-resilient distance labeling (FRDL) scheme for graphs, a simple labeling method that calculates distances between graph nodes while ignoring a predefined set of failed vertices exclusive to each query node (i.e., specific failures unique to that node). Given a set of nodes $F$ in a graph $G$, the scheme determines node pairs $(u,F)$ along with a labeling scheme such that the distance $d(v, u; F)$ is derived by counting vertices in the unique shortest path between $u$ and $v$ within the modified graph $G \setminus F$, excluding vertices in $F$. For planar graphs, our strategy employs an $O(n^2)$ scheme for node labeling and node queries. Furthermore, we extend the FRDL framework to handle edge failure scenarios. We believe these findings are of interest for graph databases, particularly those modeling physical infrastructure networks like transportation systems, which are often fault resilient and spatially representable.

Deep neural networks excel at performing complex, real-world tasks like image and speech recognition, yet they are vulnerable to adversarial attacks and susceptible to out-of distribution (OOD) inputs. Although numerous Out-of-Distribution detection methods exist, the field lacks consensus on defining OOD and evaluating OOD detectors. Consequently, current solutions often rely on heuristic approaches that sacrifice accuracy. Gaussian Processes (GPs) have previously been proposed as OOD detectors by fitting them on training data; however, their practical application is hindered by the computational burden of hyperparameter selection and scaling issues associated with large datasets. Addressing these limitations, this paper introduces a novel framework where GP strata are fitted over the unit of the input feature space to create Distributional Gaussian Processes (DGPs). These models leverage closed-form kernel functions for rapid scaling and utilize low-rank approximations alongside closed-form variational inference. Additionally, the approach utilizes closed-form predictive distributions for robust OOD detection while utilizing variational inference to estimate model uncertainty for in-domain inference. Empirical results demonstrate competitive performance against other Gaussian Process-based OOD methods. The code repository can be accessed at https://github.com/abhisheksingh1/dgp.

Pre-trained language models serve as effective zero-shot learners; however, they frequently encounter difficulties predicting attributes due to zero context representation. Astronomers have identified a low-mass active galactic nucleus (AGN) that exhibits strong flux variations across the optical and near-infrared spectra. We propose two potential causes for this behavior: intrinsic fluctuations or eruptions of the inner accretion disk, or a response of the accretion disk and starburst to stochastic nuclear luminosity changes. To evaluate these hypotheses, we constructed detailed synthetic spectra using full radiative transfer simulations of ionized gas subjected to fixed irradiation sources, which we then compared against observed spectral features and variability patterns. Our findings indicate that under constant luminosity conditions, line fluxes vary non-linearly; specifically as irradiation intensifies, broad emission line widths first expand due to increased ionization, surpassing a critical threshold before narrowing again. Our models align closely with AGN*U1's spectral evolution, confirming that its nuclear luminosity likely undergoes periodic eruptions rather than random variations. Furthermore, we estimate that black holes with masses below approximately $10^7 M_\odot$ are capable of producing such eruptions due to their low masses and relatively large Eddington ratios.

We specifically target H$\alpha$ and Mg II k emission lines to examine how the radial component of magnetic field strength varies with distance from the star across different latitudes.

This research is groundbreaking because we directly measure the slope of the surface magnetic field across the latitude circles for the first time. Using both current and future NT lines in emission, we can observe and map magnetic structures far more effectively than is currently possible with traditional thermal lines in absorption.

In the realm of Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) link prediction, evaluating dynamic models is often computationally demanding, as they require training dynamic networks alongside static models that encode entity-relational features using a graph structure like we have in TaLM. We demonstrate that dynamic network training is not only resource-intensive but also unnecessary for achieving high performance in TKG link prediction. To address this, we introduce StatFor, a method that adapts the recently developed TaLM architecture for use without a dynamic network. Statfor maintains the core strengths of TaLM while maintaining training costs comparable to conventional static models like RotatE and AMPG. Extensive evaluations on standard benchmarks show that StatFor matches the performance of state-of-the-art dynamic networks while delivering better results than traditional static models. Specifically, StatFor surpasses dynamic networks by accelerating training speeds by approximately 3.5 times and reducing overall training time.

Ultrashort pulses from oscillating lasers peak at milliwatts to Watt levels, creating severe challenges for both optical and electronic components when processing these signals at such high powers. To achieve stable, long-term operation of oscillators capable of generating milliwatt-level femtosecond pulses with a reliable, simple design, this paper offers both practical and geometrical insights into optimizing the intracavity focusing lens. Specifically, addressing oscillators operating in stable soliton and all-normal-dispersion (ANL) regimes, this research evaluates three approaches to lens positioning: (1) the standard method employed in stable resonators, (2) an extended approach utilizing a large magnification setup, and the (3) a hybrid strategy combining the classical and extended techniques. Under strictly nonlinear and non-critical conditions, the ANL regime is proven to be more resilient against minor fluctuations in active element thickness compared to the classical configuration and features a smaller Kerr sensitivity coefficient. Consequently, the optimal strategy for building a robust, simple oscillating laser is to select the classical setup and optimize positioning via maximum lens magnification to fully exploit the advantages of the ANL regime.

Detecting wildfires early is vital for preventing forest fires and safeguarding human lives and infrastructure. Although Deep Learning-based algorithms have significantly advanced active surveillance, there remains a lack of fire detection solutions specifically for multi-spectral infrared-visible imagery that can be deployed in real-world settings without needing target localization data. In this study, we introduce a new unsupervised Deep Learning framework called FIRe-GAN (Fire Integration-GAN), designed to synthesize realistic fire masks from infrared inputs while simultaneously fusing infrared-visible pairs to amplify visible signs of combustion. FIRe-GAN utilizes two Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) trained on paired data to generate a unified output through adversarial learning. By leveraging the high contrast of fire in infrared bands and the strong semantic information of fire visible images, our method produces integrated images of superior quality compared to existing techniques, demonstrating superior performance in practical application.

Depression is a prevalent and costly mental health issue that frequently manifests through postings on social media platforms. Although machine learning methods have been investigated to detect depression from online content, they are hindered by the absence of both the quantity and quality of available datasets, which severely restricts the creation of large-scale systems. Addressing this gap, we present a systematic methodology for building dependable depression datasets, followed by an analysis of current models applied to the newly constructed data. Extensive experiments were conducted using four well-known social media platforms, yielding significant findings. Our results indicate that Ensemble Learning achieved an F1-score of 81.2%, outperforming Support Vector Machines (SVM) at 73.8% and Deep Learning (DL) at 73.8% accuracy. Furthermore, we observed trends suggesting that networks with more active user engagement tend to generate higher classification accuracy.

This study introduces and analyzes stick-slip behavior within feedback-regulated control systems that incorporate Coulomb friction at the output stage. By modeling friction via discontinuous sign functions at output positions, these systems present significant analytical challenges. We establish a framework designed to demonstrate convergence to steady-state solutions or to enter periodic oscillations—either sticking or slip modes. Our analysis proves that under specific conditions, closed-loop systems either stabilize into a fixed solution or settle into a limit cycle without spontaneously developing new forms of stick-slip friction. To validate this theory using an example cart-pole configuration, we integrate the Harmonic Balance Method with a Haar wavelet approximation to construct a robust numerical approach for addressing non-linear switching systems featuring Coulomb friction.

This study investigates a policy optimization challenge for policyholders utilizing deep Q-networks (DQN) within a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework. While this approach appears straightforward, the authors demonstrate that even for DQN-enhanced utility maximization, achieving computational tractability is difficult; consequently, they introduce a novel method to address this difficulty. Specifically, they derive an explicit formula for the DQN-enhanced Q-value, which circumvents the standard DQN iterative update step typically required to approximate these functions. This innovation leads to an efficient algorithm capable of rapidly locating utility-maximizing policies by directly optimizing the parameters of the Q-function rather than iterating updates. The methodology demonstrates broad utility not only in the maximization of expected returns but also in the minimization of capital-to-profit ratios for insurance firms and the optimization of premium rates for those companies.

Sequential models are widely employed in recommender systems to forecast a user's upcoming actions by analyzing their interaction history; however, these examples typically rely on implicit activity labels that often require extensive creation and maintenance efforts. To address this limitation, this research introduces Latent User Purpose (LUP), an approach designed to automatically discover hidden interaction intents. By modeling interactions as first-order Markov chains, LUP is trained to assign probabilities to potential user activities. Unlike the limitations of existing alternatives, a key advantage of this method is its ability to scale effectively for both scenarios where specific interaction labels are already known and those where all possible user objectives must be deduced from data. Consequently, LUP supports the generation of novel implicit activity tags without manual annotation requirements. We have integrated this methodology into LUP4LACE, a comprehensive dataset and benchmark for monitoring hidden activity purposes within recommendation engines. Extensive testing validates LUP's effectiveness in generating accurate predictions and demonstrates its utility in enhancing the performance of standard sequential algorithms through data augmentation techniques.

This research investigates the decentralized management of linear time-invariant (LTI) systems involving multi-channel configurations. It first establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for a system's stabilizability via the use of various output feedback mechanisms, specifically examining single output, subset output, and frequency-regional output scenarios. Subsequently, it addresses the task of decentralized control structure design, demonstrating that if a model-based controller utilizing the full set of input channels exists for system stabilization, then an algorithm exists to construct a viable network of controllers, each stabilizing just a single channel. This algorithm relies on solving an initial stabilizing controller problem and subsequently refining it to formulate stabilizer gains for each individual channel in an exact manner. Furthermore, it proves that under this framework, no loop closure sequence leads to instability. The paper also notes that, apart from cases where only a single output feedback mechanism works, simultaneous stabilization is not required. In the context of systems with output feedback, each channel is rigorously designed to maintain stability regardless of any closure sequence or any combination of output channels that might be used. Additionally, it demonstrates that by utilizing control structure information along with a specific stabilizing controller, we can develop a management system enabling systems to dynamically switch between different channel configurations without compromising overall stability.

The rapid spread of the SARS-CoV-2 virus has precipitated a worldwide pandemic, resulting in millions of confirmed cases and hundreds of thousands of fatalities. Accurately detecting this virus is vital for preventing further transmission and alleviating the societal devastation caused. Although numerous diagnostic tests have been introduced, many remain constrained by scarcity of resources, unavailable infrastructure, or prohibitive costs. Reinforcement learning theories describe how the brain learns to navigate complex decision-making tasks by relying on a set of optimal algorithms, yet specific tactics that deviate from these optimal strategies may still offer advantages like enhanced flexibility. This study explores whether such non-optimal tactics are merely random variations or if they are inherited traits that some individuals use more effectively than others. We demonstrate that in a difficult, dynamic control task, the non-optimal strategy of "demon memory"—which entails retaining the outcomes of others' actions—is strongly tied to dopamine release as measured by fMRI. Our findings reveal that demonstrating the extent to which an action leads to a particular reward predicts inter-individual differences in midbrain dopamine activation during this non-optimal strategy. Importantly, the degree to which an action leads to a particular reward predicts human differences in responding to the fMRI study.

This text outlines a set of proposals for generating quantum entanglement and contextuality by applying complex $E_8$ matrix elements to a core quantum system. This study examines the approximate Frechet distance framework for data streams with time indices. Although it is well-established that the Frechet distance between two polygonal chains of $n$ vertices is $\Theta(n)$ in the exact setting, we present algorithms for approximate close neighbor searching that operate in sublinear time, contingent on the spatio-temporal characteristics of the input data. Our approach leverages index structures that enable rapid rejection of non-similar series and accelerate discovery of similarity when applicable. Consequently, depending on the series' properties, our methods can reduce search times from the linear $\mathcal{O}(n)$ complexity to either $n^{1/2}$, $\log n$, or even constant levels. We validate our approach empirically against the state-of-the-art techniques that rely on low-level distance proxying using multiple subsampling strategies. Our results indicate that these proposed approaches substantially outperform existing methods across various benchmark collections drawn from diverse practical domains. Furthermore, we introduce a theoretical bound limiting the sample complexity required for exact performance under specific time-weighted metrics and provide proof that the novel algorithms surpass these theoretical limits.

In contemporary large-scale superconducting processors, cumulative measurement errors frequently cause errors in a bitstring's most likely to flip from its true state, thereby necessitating iterative Bayesian unfolding to correct the bitstring post-measurement. This letter details the scalable implementation of such correction on a quantum device itself. Our strategy links the complex, qubit-specific amplitude and phase parameters to a compact set of classical effective two-qubit measurement error matrices (EMEMs). These EMEMs are derived using a minimal number of specialized calibration runs. By mapping the nonlinear relationship between EMEMs and the underlying quantum parameters, this approach enables the correction to function without requiring frequent recalibrations. Validated on the IBM Tokyo processor (127 physical qubits), this method yielded approximately a tenfold reduction in observable bitstring entropy.

This study addresses robot-to-human communication, specifically focusing on conveying action execution criteria to a user interface. In a shared autonomy setting, a human observes the robot's partial autonomy to better understand the connection between robot actions and their standards. The method prioritizes the selection of actions that reveal standards most clearly, balancing efficiency against informative value, and also determines less clear-cut robot moves to maintain performance. Evaluations in a 2D grid world demonstrate substantial gains in both robot performance and user satisfaction regarding standard comprehension. Additionally, tests in a real-world kitchen environment confirm the method's feasibility for physical robot applications.

Driven by the growing demand for autonomous systems in uncharted territories, this work introduces a new navigation architecture that synthesizes global planning and local path tracking. At its core, a hierarchical topological map guides the agent at the strategic level, while a feature-rich curvature algorithm executes path rendering and smoothing at the tactical level to ensure smooth adherence. Designed for robust real-time computation, the hierarchical component is implemented in C++ using an efficient implementation of the Fast Marches algorithm. Meanwhile, the trajectory-following module, written in ROS/Python, leverages the Curvature Algorithm to smooth and optimize local movement. Together, these complementary approaches are demonstrated in a simulated scenario involving a robot exploring a completely unknown environment.

Numerous research efforts have recently focused on constructing code sets with low peak-to-average power ratio (PACP) for multi-carrier code division multiple access (MC-CDMA) systems by utilizing orthogonal complementary sequences (OCS). This study presents new OCS constructions defined by multivariable math functions. Specifically, we prove that our constructed sequences exhibit good auto- and cross-correlation characteristics if specific conditions are met among these functions. Additionally, we describe methods to expand codes into inter-group complementary code sets with improved performance and detail strategies for forming Zi-two-dimensional (3D) array codes with zero imaginary parts (2D-Z-Array) possessing flat range spectra. These new OCS families significantly outperform existing counterparts in terms of PAPR reduction.

Computed Tomography (CT) imaging serves as a vital diagnostic tool in medical care and an essential modality for material characterization within various engineering fields. This study extends conventional CT reconstruction by incorporating multi-energetic X-ray spectra to simultaneously reconstruct materials and decompose them based on the CT sensors' available data. Evaluating both noise performance across multiple reconstructions is critical when accounting for varying X-ray energy levels captured by CT sensors during material visualization processes. Consequently, we introduce a comprehensive model optimization framework capable of handling noise within CT sensors under polyenergetic X-ray exposure conditions while utilizing a novel non-convex noise model that effectively represents diverse exposure spectrums across different scanning scenarios in material characterization workflows. This study demonstrates superior performance compared with conventional methods, showing significant improvements over existing noise models used in clinical settings for material visualization applications using multi-view x-ray imaging systems

While the spill-out mechanism and nonlocal behavior, both of which tend to reduce the metallic region's effective plasma density, generally lower the optical confinement of gap-plasmons, significant discrepancies between predictions based on these two mechanisms arise only at a specific quantum turnaround point. This transition occurs when the gap width shifts from a regime where spill-out and nonlocal effects expand into each other, allowing them to reinforce one another, to one where they operate in distinct zones over the interface where they act independently.

Visualizing multivariate time series (mTSTS) and longitudinal datasets is difficult given the complexity involved, yet current visualization techniques often fail to engage users effectively. To achieve this, we developed an interface allowing participants to manually adjust control parameters (marked as $X$ controls) during viewing, which they can decide to modify or keep constant. By analyzing how participants interacted with these $X$ controls, we derived their ideal data-analytic settings. To demonstrate the viability of this method, the author created a interface to assist individuals not only in quickening specific control parameters but also in handling unspecified variables efficiently. Our findings indicate that this method serves as a practical approach for enhancing engagement when dealing with longitudinal and multivariate temporal data.

Applying machine learning to Electronic Health Records (EHRs) presents unique hurdles, primarily due to an imbalance between a vast number of available features (features often exceeding data instances) and scarce labeled examples. Although Heterogeneous Association Rules (HARs) have previously been used to uncover significant associations by leveraging heterogeneous knowledge, extending these models directly to Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) faces substantial difficulties due to Heterogeneous Records' (HRs) inherent complexity, which necessitates the integration of multiple data modalities. To address these EHR-based challenges, this study introduces the Heterogeneous Resemblance Graph Neural Network (HRGNN), a new technique for classifying patients based on the heterogeneous similarity of their records. The core of this method lies in the Heterogeneous Resemblance Layer (HRL), a dedicated component for computing similarity between records containing heterogeneous nodes. The HRGNN subsequently trains a GNN model, defined on HRs, using these computed resemblances. Evaluated on an isolated hospital section's EHR data, the approach achieved an AUC score of 0.815 for sepsis detection. These findings demonstrate that the HRGNN is effective in managing the intricate complexities of heterogeneous medical records.

Scan matching serves as a fundamental component within autonomous systems, facilitating map construction and localization. In typical implementations using LiDAR-based depth scans, point clouds are aligned through Iterative Closest Point (ICP) by minimizing the Euclidean distance between corresponding points. This paper introduces an ICP variant biased toward distribution probabilities within point cloud pairs rather than individual points. To achieve this, a Deep Neural Network filters these probability distributions before the optimization stage. Evaluation results indicate that the filtered bias effectively scans matching distributions instead of singular points and enhances robustness against motion blur. Furthermore, because the method prioritizes overall data distribution characteristics, it precludes the requirement for a characteristic point cloud in alignment. Avoiding this dependency prevents biasing toward specific features, thereby ensuring robustness against environmental changes in subsequent alignments.

Satellite imagery plays a critical role in monitoring changes to Earth's surface, particularly for detecting infrastructure developments like buildings and roads essential for urban planning. While current satellite-based image processing typically relies on deep learning, it necessitates extensive annotated training data and remains vulnerable to distribution shifts across different regions. We introduce a deep-learning-free approach leveraging geoscientific principles that relies solely on accessible open-source data intrinsic to the input images. This method utilizes a precomputed, publicly available land surface mask to filter out non-relevant areas such as oceans or deserts, thereby narrowing the search focus. Additionally, by analyzing band ratios in the image data, it enhances contrast between potential building areas and surrounding land features to further refine detection accuracy.

This method successfully replicates key spectral features across various energy regions, including high-fluence effects like electron stimulation and satellite structures, without adjusting any free parameters. Consequently, this approach offers a robust foundation for developing quantitative analysis tools for non-linear XANES phenomena.

This research introduces a framework for detecting inaccuracies in dynamical systems modeled by machine learning. By training an algorithm on the residual errors of the initial model, a corrective model is generated to enhance a refined, iterative correction process. Applying this approach to long-term predictions of the Earth system, we successfully leveraged our method to forecast the stratospheric polar vortex response to major stratospheric sudden warmings (SSWs). Our findings demonstrate that the algorithm effectively captures key characteristics of this response, offering potential for volitional modeling of the response mechanism. Furthermore, the algorithm's ability to learn the timing of an event's onset enables the integration of a timing constraint without requiring explicit input of temporal data or additional training.

Massive stars typically emerge from the collapse of dense cores, and their formation is inextricably linked to the evolutionary stages of dark molecular clouds. This research investigates the connection between core evolution and star birth by analyzing dark molecular clouds in the Galactic Center region. Using a combination of $J$, $K_s$, and $8~\mu$m emission maps from the GLIMPPE survey alongside $8~\mu$m extinction data from Nisbet et al. (2017), the authors reconstructed a three-dimensional mass map of dark molecular clouds within the Dragon Nebula ($NGC\ 6334h$-II). Through the application of the MESA core model (Bressan et al. 2010), the study classified cores into three categories based on their mass and evolutionary state (distinguishing between core contraction and expansion phases). Results indicate an expanding massive core located within DR2 (a distinct region within NGC 6334h-II). Although this study primarily targets the DR2 core, evidence suggests that core expansion within NGD 6334h-II may precede star formation. Additionally, the analysis confirms a strong correlation between core mass and radius across all classified cores. These findings suggest that core expansion could signal an environment conducive to forming new stars in the DR2 region.

This paper introduces a straightforward method for computing rates of collision among primordial black holes (PBHs) considered as dark matter by utilizing PopSyCLE, a code originally designed for stellar binary dynamics. Within this framework, PBHs are treated as compact objects that form pairs through gravitational interactions, allowing the statistical distribution of these interactions to be modeled via established methodologies. Key parameters, including mass distribution spectra, formation rates, and gravitational wave background signatures from early universe PBH mergers, are integrated into the approach. We also address the thermodynamic evolution of the universe and the mechanisms governing the creation and subsequent dilution of the PBH population as cosmic expansion proceeds. By leveraging an analytical expression for the distribution function and numerical integration through PopSyCLE, we calculate both the commissive number density and the time-resolved collision frequency of PBHs throughout history. We further explore constraints on PBH dark matter status for masses below $10^{4-M_{\odot}}$, utilizing bounds derived from the lifetime of the most distant observed galaxy, Elysium (Elsar), which constrains how many PBHs could survive within that early environment.

This study examines a novel phase characterized by one-dimensional splay modulation found in systems of hard, triangular wedges. Because these triangular wedges can be modeled as spherically connected dimers, we anticipate similar physical behaviors in a new class of colloidal colloids, referred to here as "bimodal colloids." These consist of two fused spherical components arranged in a linear configuration, which also results in triangular shape when viewed as hard particles. These results further illustrate emerging physics associated with non-spherical colloids, which opens up new possibilities for applications.

Although large language models (LLMs) offer versatile capabilities, fine-tuning them fully is costly in terms of both time and money, especially when creating domain-specific versions for specific tasks. To address this, researchers have explored parameter-efficient techniques, primarily focusing on adapting only the prompt parameters within the model's intermediate layers. However, since these approaches retain most original tokens capable of generating undesired outputs in standard applications, they often result in compromised performance for specific domains. This paper introduces a novel strategy—Special Token Adaptation (STA)—which involves learning to reclassify certain output tokens into unique special tokens and subsequently guiding the model to generate these new tokens for specific concepts or phrases. Experiments across various benchmark tasks demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms comparable baselines while requiring minimal additional training parameters.

This work investigates two solution methods for adding preference sets: pure preference addition (PCA) and context-based preference addition (PCA). This study presents a theoretical investigation into the ground state of a weakly interacting boson gas subjected to confinement, where interactions are modulated by a parameter $r_s$. As $r_s$ increases from small to large values, the system undergoes a boson-fermion crossover, evolving from a standard Bose-Einstein condensate to an uncondensed state characterized by Pauli exclusion. Notably, both phenomena can be described using a unified theoretical framework involving two distinct length scales: $l_r$, which represents the ratio between interaction and confinement strengths ($r_s/l_r$), and $l_0$, the thermal de Broglie wavelength. At high values of $r_s$, the system exhibits oscillatory behavior akin to that of an ideal Fermi gas; however, as $r_s$ decreases, these oscillations are suppressed and converge to the properties of a non-interacting Bose-Einstein condensate.

While many empirical studies have underscored the prevalence of test smells, little attention has focused on their actual impact from the point of view of software engineering professionals. This study addresses this gap by examining how software engineers evaluate test smell severity. Through a case study approach, the research methods included administering three successive questionnaires to gauge how developers assess issues regarding test functionality and aesthetic quality, alongside conducting thematic coding of group interviews regarding these evaluations. The findings indicate that perceived severity regarding test quality varies among developers; however, assessments related to test aesthetics remain consistent. The study's contribution lies in offering actionable insights for researchers and tools for future engineering techniques based on these findings. Significantly, it represents a pioneering effort combining empirical inquiry with practical engagement of professional developers regarding their evaluation of test code quality issues.

We introduce a multi-stage deep generative framework designed to learn hierarchical feature representations optimized for diverse tasks. Our method employs a stacked architecture of conditional generative models, where each level employs an energy-based model to generate features conditioned on level-specific and higher-level latent variables, creating dependencies across all levels. This framework encompasses a wide variety of probabilistic models, such as those with Sinkhorn divengences as variational objectives—effectively covering energy-based models, normalizing flows, and more—as well as methods guided by task-specific fine-tuning. These tasks, formulated as discriminative models over the learned latents within the generative space via variational objectives like discriminative lower bounds, enable generative pre-training. This approach facilitates generating robust intermediate representations through variational objective minimization, serving as strong starting points for fine-tuning on specific downstream tasks.

Identifying and isolating contacts is central to managing infectious disease outbreaks, though the effectiveness of contact tracing relies heavily on accurate contact data. In July 2021, UK authorities launched a new initiative allowing individuals to log face-to-face interactions lasting 30 minutes or more via a smartphone app alongside government-led enforcement. To assess its influence, a simulation modeled these enforcement measures against a baseline scenario that excluded trace enforcement. These simulations, which incorporated varying levels of SARS-CoV-2 transmission rates, contact volumes, and background herd immunity levels, revealed key findings. When transmission rates were typical of pre-vaccine conditions, trace enforcement boosted the power of app-based tracking, increasing app-driven infections by up to 58% compared to baseline scenarios. However, during high transmission rates similar to those observed post-vaccination, this enhancement dropped significantly to less than 20%. Furthermore, while the baseline already drove trace partners toward more individuals, trace enforcement shifted partners toward driving infections from non-vaccinated individuals, highlighting that enforcement gains diminish as background transmission rises.

In robotic vision, extrinsic calibration is vital for determining the camera's position and orientation relative to its image sensor. Although this process is standard in vision tasks, robots frequently suffer from calibration errors due to mechanical wear, mechanical shocks, and impacts. Addressing these drifts is critical, particularly in eye-in-hand configurations, where the camera is rigidly attached to the robot's end-effector. In this setup, even slight mechanical perturbations can cause significant image projection inaccuracies. We propose a technique for rapid and low-cost extrinsic parameter realignment driven by deep neural networks, utilizing just two images to train the system. By leveraging the sparse training data alongside large-scale perturbations, the model learns to estimate the camera's transformation matrix based on visual discrepancies. Furthermore, by injecting controlled noise into the training dataset, the model gains robustness across various camera fields of view. Experimental evaluations confirm that the proposed system successfully adapts to simulated perturbations and executes effective calibration on real image sequences.

This study addresses the challenge of inverse constrained reinforcement learning (RCRL), an area that simultaneously determines the objective reward function and constraint parameters to align the resulting agent policy with a predefined set of behaviors. While prior work focused primarily on reward learning, we focus here on determining optimal constraint parameters through three key contributions. First, we demonstrate that RCRL can be mathematically transformed into finding a solution within a polytope, a process that involves formulating a series of constrained optimization problems. Second, we introduce a practical polynomial-time algorithm designed to find the value that best aligns the learned constraints with the inductive biases of the environment's reward structure. Third, we evaluate our method on a range of tasks involving both offline and online data, covering both discrete and continuous state-spaces. Results indicate that our approach excelss at identifying and recovering the true underlying constraint parameters.

GAIA is designed to conduct the most comprehensive astrometric survey of the Milky Way ever undertaken. Operating as a space-based mission within the optical spectrum (430–700 nm), it captures high-precision positional and motion data for approximately 10 billion stars, alongside photometry for an even larger sample of one billion. The data includes precise measurements of positions and proper motions extending to roughly 8 kpc in radius. To achieve these goals, GAIA employs a novel telescope architecture featuring two integrated telescopes situated within a single optical bench, complemented by advanced photometric techniques that deliver exceptional accuracy and reliability.

Brain network research relies heavily on graph theory, utilizing both measured and modeled networks where vertices serve as brain areas and connections represent functional or structural dependencies. Existing network analysis predominantly relies on functional and structural correlation coefficients, yet these linear metrics fail to adequately capture the full complexity of network interactions. This limitation has driven the development of sophisticated modeling methods, such as dynamic causal modeling, to infer causal brain networks. Despite advancements, these approaches face a significant limitation: the difficulty in comparing results across methods that use different network definitions due to these linear metrics. To address this challenge, the present work introduces a novel network construction method grounded in weighted directed clustering. Unlike previous techniques, this framework applies unified principles across network types that vary in definition, measurement, or theoretical construction. Specifically, we developed a framework capable of processing network data with any combination of directionality, node count, connection density, or interaction nature (excitatory or inhibitory). Central to this method is the optimization of free parameters, allowing a single set of settings to generate network structures effective whether used for inferred models or measured networks. Empirical validation demonstrates the method's robustness by successfully reproducing the core architecture of real functional networks and specific structures from simulation studies. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion on parameter selection strategies and provide open-source implementations to facilitate broader adoption in brain network research.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) integrate physical laws into data-driven machine learning models. Our research focuses on deriving a general framework to certify and estimate the posteriori estimation of methodological mistakes inherent in PINNs. By deriving rigorous error bounds grounded in physics and numerical findings, our method assesses and compares the performance of PINNs against other standard techniques. Consequently, our system quantifies how physical constraints influence model accuracy in light of empirical evidence.

This study establishes novel multivariate regression models to determine the concentration of air pollutants as a function of time, while accounting for temporal dependencies and spatial variations. The spatial and temporal health effects of these pollutants on blood pressure were examined using two distinct statistical methods: Geostatistics and machine learning.

Gapped graphene possesses a conventional valley Hall effect in which a transverse velocity proportional to a non-zero Berry curvature emerges from an effective mass gap. In contrast, we demonstrate that this phenomenon can be achieved in clean, monolayer graphene—which lacks a Berry curvature—by utilizing a static electric field across a substrate. This orbital analogue of the Hall effect arises from a non-collinear spin texture generated by a combination of a substrate-induced mass term and exchange coupling to that spin texture. Notably, carrier transport occurs without a magnetic field, rendering the effect robust against artifacts related to spurious fields. These characteristics suggest significant potential applications in spintronics, valleytronics, and related technologies.

Recent research highlights the vulnerability of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to adversarial attacks in data contamination scenarios, where adversaries introduce subtle anomalies into training datasets to force GNNs into generating highly misleading outputs. Building on this vulnerability, we introduce an attack framework that leverages principles from reinforcement learning to successfully contaminate graph-based machine learning models. We evaluate our approach using benchmark datasets ranging from traditional machine learning sets to increasingly sophisticated community and physical benchmarks. Additionally, we explore the impact of employing a specific readout mechanism designed to aggregate graph node information into GNNs. Our findings indicate that our proposed method achieves success rates of approximately 90% across all tested datasets, consistently outperforming baseline comparison attacks by significant margins in every scenario.

The development of astrometric catalogs is primarily driven by the analysis of blue and green magnitudes alongside astrometric data. However, photometric information extends further into the near-infrared spectrum. This study addresses a methodological challenge: improving the linking of candidate stars via a new, low-cost algorithm that incorporates a broader photometric range. The technique utilizes astrometric offsets, photometric color distributions, and explicit distance metrics to establish probabilistic reliability scores for candidate pairings. The methodology was evaluated against established data, such as Gaia DR3 and the second catalog from the Pan-STARRS1 Redshift Survey Project, demonstrating its efficacy in astrometric catalog merging processes.

Concepts and their relations are fundamental to ontology, yet traditional tools like Protégé, generally featuring tree- or network-based interfaces visualize only isolated fragments and fail to effectively handle entire ontologies. The high computational cost of deep neural networks often limits their real-time application on resource-constrained robots. To overcome this, we introduce an active framework for optimizing neural networks specifically for robot navigation tasks. Our approach involves integrating navigation with model training, allowing the robot to identify regions requiring refinement and prioritize sampling in those areas. This environment-aware sampling is further enhanced through a strategy that exploits temporal dynamics. Additionally, by formulating an explicit multi-objective reward function, we demonstrate that this framework successfully generalizes from simulated to real-world settings. Experimental evaluations on both simulation and physical platforms confirm that this method yields significantly faster convergence compared to standard baselines. The research provides a robust mechanism for deploying deep learning models across various platforms, such as autonomous vehicles and drones.

Active Brownian particles (ABPs) are commonly used to model systems exhibiting the Soret effect, where a temperature gradient induces a thermal drift leading to particle separation. In scenarios with interaction-induced sorting, an ABP model featuring internal degrees of freedom demonstrates a significant Soret coefficient compared to those without. Although prior research established the principle that decoupling this internal degree of movement from overall translation enhances the Soret response, this mechanism remained unexplained until now. By employing both numerical simulations and theoretical analysis, this study elucidates such a model's contribution to the enhanced Soret efficiency, focusing on active binary mixtures containing charged and neutral components. Furthermore, leveraging theoretical insights allows for optimizing the design of micro- and macro-scale mixing devices that utilize active particles to improve industrial operational efficiency under thermal conditions.

Graded essays are treated as Text-to-Text input-output pairs to train large language models that generate scores for student writing. Our simple yet highly effective proof-of-concept employs an open-source fine-tuned pre-trained large language model utilizing the recently introduced Deberta architecture. We demonstrate that this model performs as a single-shot evaluator, producing evaluations in the style of "1/10" without necessitating an additional head or any post-processing steps. Finally, our results demonstrate the model is able to replicate human scoring patterns closely, outperforming smaller existing models significantly better.

Adapting detectors trained on one domain to another remains a significant challenge, largely due to false positives arising from artifacts like noise and uneven illumination. Through a novel approach that decouples positive and negative relaxation, the model effectively identifies unreliable detections in a fully self-supervised manner. Comprehensive evaluation on the CityPersons benchmark demonstrates the superiority of Box Re-Rank over existing pedestrian tracking techniques, establishing new state-of-the-art results in reducing false positives.

This research investigates the consequences associated with varying release points during throwing actions.

The authors present **FauxThrow**, an instrument designed with a customizable throwing workspace aimed at examining technical proficiency in throwing tasks. This tool incorporates advanced tracking technologies—specifically an optical motion-capture system combined with inertial measurement units—to precisely record critical parameters such as point of release, release angle, ball path velocity, and ball trajectory. Through this methodology, users and researchers can execute complex tasks involving both small and large movements. The tool facilitates quantitative and qualitative assessments of throw performance by modeling optimal release points using 2D and 3D biomechanical geometries of the hand. Additionally, it evaluates throw precision by calculating standard deviations to measure consistency within repeated small movements and accuracy relative to a designated target for larger movements. The tool also scrutinizes the biomechanics of the gesture by monitoring joint kinematics and kinematics data to quantify total energy generated by various body joints. Results indicate that inaccurate release points lead to reduced task accuracy and heightened joint stress, suggesting potential risk factors regarding throwing techniques. Thus, FauxThrow offers a comprehensive research platform capable of quantitatively and qualitatively examining the impacts stemming from a misplaced release point across diverse throwing activities.

Neural machine translation relies on encoder-decoders capable of generating sequences of words; however, these models lack any inherent structural capability, resulting in outputs that may exhibit grammatical errors. We instead investigate a top-down approach combining a structured decoder with a sequence decoder to translate into a forest representing multiple syntactic hypotheses and their constituent structures. Our hypothesis is that the potential captured in syntactic structures will enhance word-level translations to avoid mistakes. Evidence supports this view, as our method outperforms both a sequence-only baseline and the current state-of-the-art on multiple languages. Additionally, the generated data, including these links between structure and text, was used for semi-supervised parsing, yielding further improvements.

This study introduces a new, scalable strategy for computing shallow linear shadows, a technique that approximates local mathematical expectations and mitigates complex circuit complications inherent in standard shadow methods. The approach involves sampling from distributions generated by random quantum circuits with only minimal circuit depth. Notably, employing shallow linear shadows enables the efficient estimation of local mathematical expectations, including those found in ground states, using circuits impractically difficult for standard shadow techniques. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that shallow linear shadows accurately capture Hamiltonian expectation values even under substantial noise conditions, suggesting they could effectively monitor quantum computers during actual operational runs.

While many researchers use the Sibyl model to detect malicious users in social networks, it remains underexplored as a tool to improve user-generated text. This study introduces an adaptation of Sibyl specifically for enhancing the accuracy of unsupervised text classification. We focus on two key issues: the unreliable nature of labels assigned to training documents of minimal length and the model's vulnerability to outliers that skew class probabilities to incorrect categories. Our solution introduces modifications to Sibyl that significantly enhance robustness, yielding marked performance gains, particularly in two-dimensional tasks. Our results offer the strongest evidence to date for unsupervised, two-dimensional text clustering and highlight the necessity of removing identified outliers from training datasets.

Representational Discontinuity Theory posits that cognitive limitations stem from representational constraints within neural frameworks. Research indicates that nonlinear deep learning setups often fail to sustain the strict linearity of Wernicke-Wichwunder models, leading researchers to explore methods that can train neural layers capable producing linear representational hierarchies without compromising performance. We introduce a meta-learning framework designed to conduct this objective utilizing supervised data via pseudo-Wichwunder analysis—a novel technique for quantifying representation linearity. Empirical evaluations on a binary classification task involving ImageNet demonstrate a successful transition from typical nonlinear hierarchical architectures to a classification-adjacent linear matrix derived via Wishworth analysis. Furthermore, we examine the linearity of representations across multiple neural networks, including a parameter refinement strategy and data augmentation protocols used to boost classification results. These findings underscore that both the quality and linearity of these representations are paramount in determining overall model efficacy.

Although machine translation (MT) has advanced significantly, translating low-resource and rare languages remains challenging. To address this, we need to develop very compact yet effective MT models. While knowledge distillation and quantization are widely used to create smaller, lighter models, they are often applied sequentially to model compression techniques, yet the impact of quantization as part of knowledge distillation remains largely underexplored. In this study, we investigate both the efficacy and reliability of combining these methods within diverse linguistic scenarios. Our findings reveal a critical limitation: when a quantum MT model is trained using a teacher enriched through knowledge distillation, it frequently fails to match the teacher's performance, yielding outputs that are less fluent and coherent than unquantized models trained directly. Furthermore, we demonstrate that such performance degradation is particularly pronounced when the teacher comes from a large-scale model covering many low-resource languages. Consequently, our research urges the MT community to exercise extreme caution when integrating quantization and knowledge distillation, as doing so can lead to unreliable outcomes for translating low-resource languages.

Deep learning models typically demand vast amounts of labeled data; however, gathering such annotations is often prohibitively expensive and labor-intensive, creating significant hurdles for clinical deployment. In this study, we investigate how reducing training dataset size affects model performance, specifically addressing challenges related to limited data availability in medical imaging. We evaluate three augmentation strategies designed to generate additional training samples by transforming existing labeled images. The findings demonstrate that substantial performance gains can be achieved when these augmentation techniques are applied, particularly when the initial training set is small, underscoring their utility in lowering the specific data collection burden required for model training.

Although image captioning is considered a well-established task, current models struggle to generate varied descriptions when processing the same input due to limited training data variety or rigid model architectures. To address this, we propose a novel framework that controls captioning output using natural language prompts, leveraging extensive multi-language training data to enable generation of diverse styles for a single image. Our approach involves no modifications to standard decoders, requiring only training data adjusted with these controlled prompts. Additionally, we introduce a novel attention mechanism that enhances control precision by focusing on relevant features within the encoder's intermediate layers. Extensive experiments across various datasets and challenging settings—such as zero-shot scenarios—demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.
